matters.text:
7.F Contract No. SP545-22 Law Enforcement Services for Metrolink - Exercise Option 2
    and Increase Contract Authority - Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department

    Mr. Konczal requested additional contract authority to continue law enforcement services
    through June 30, 2027. This contract extension is requested to ensure continuity of
    operations through the upcoming 2026 FIFA World Cup. The LASD Metrolink Bureau is
    leading the efforts in coordinating law enforcement response for this event.

    Director Tettemer asked if these contracts are scalable and if these contracts can be
    modified if there is potential for a service reduction.

    Mr. Konczal stated when Metrolink increased service more officers were not requested so
    staffing levels are the same pre- and post-COVID. Crime has been reduced down 51%
    over the last year but the contracts are scalable and if service is cut, staff can look at
    redeployment if there are any reductions that can be taken with law enforcement. He added
    there is a requirement to patrol and secure the right-of-way with regards to trespassers
    and deputies do fare enforcement regardless of service.

    Second Vice-Chair Trembley asked with respect to this particular agreement if the portion
    of the amendment attributable to the FIFA event has been quantified.

    Mr. Konczal confirmed in their normal course of duties staff has been attending FIFA
    meetings and coordinating with LA Metro and attending meetings with other stakeholders
    but it hasn’t been quantified yet.

    Second Vice-Chair Trembley asked if the amount referenced in the previous item was
    intended to cover the anticipated security costs.

    Mk. Kettle affirmed they have funded 30 deputies for World Cup activity and will be able to
    augment with around $160,000 that was received separately for private security.

    Second Vice-Chair Trembley requested the ad hoc Olympic Committee reconvene and
    receive information if there will there be separate contracts with the security agencies
    relative to Olympics security. He asked how soon until that contract is ultimately before this
    Board and he hoped that information can come back to the ad hoc committee at the
    soonest.

    ACTION: Upon a single motion by Director Barger and seconded by Second Vice-Chair
    Trembley, the Board (11-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to amend Contract No.
    SP545-22 with the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department (LASD) for Law Enforcement
    Services to exercise Option 2 through June 30, 2027, and increase the contract authority
    in the amount of $4,333,986 for FY27. This will increase the total contract authority from
    $53,816,490 to $58,150,476.

    The amounts for which contract authority is requested are included in, and are contingent
    upon, the adoption of the Proposed FY27 Operating Budget.




                                                                                                     801
                                               12

7.G Contract No. EP247-26 - Oxnard Accident Car and Out-Of-Service Car Rehabilitation
    - Recommendation to Award - SYSTRA Canada

    Rolling Stock Engineering Manager II DK Ha stated the Authority intends to rehabilitate 19
    coach and cab railcars that are currently out-of-service. Four of the cars were heavily
    damaged in February 2015 in a collision with a truck that resulted in the cars derailing. The
    other 15 cars are out-of-service due to multiple components that are obsolete, damages
    due to accidents, or vandalism. The purpose of this project is to rehabilitate the cars and
    return them to revenue service as soon as possible.

    Director Wapner asked about the timing on the repairs and when Metrolink will get the cars
    back.

    Mr. Ha stated on the current schedule all 19 cars can be returned into service by March
    2028. He confirmed they will be returned as they are completed.

    Director Spiegel noted March of 2028 is not going to help the current mechanical issues.

    Mr. Kettle agreed but shared there have been vast improvements over the last 3-4 months
    related to equipment with Alstom’s extra staffing and the effort to get parts and materials.

    Second Vice-Chair Trembley asked about the mention that the project was 100% funded
    by the FTA in the staff report.

    Mr. Ha stated there are two funding sources: member agency funds and settlement funds.

    Chief of Program Delivery Justin Fornelli clarified there is an inaccurate statement in the report
    and the funding for this program is both settlement funds from the Oxnard accident and State
    of Good Repair funds as part of the capital budget which is funded through the FTA.

    Second Vice-Chair Trembley noted there is only one bidder and asked if any bid protests
    will be received.

    Senior Contract and Compliance Administrator Dorothea Cantero explained at this time
    there is no bid protest and there were letters submitted for no bid from other vendors.

    Director Sandoval asked how much a brand-new rail and cab car costs.

    Mr. Ha stated a brand-new purchase is roughly around $3.7M per car.

    ACTION: Upon a single motion by Second Vice-Chair Trembley and seconded by Director
    McCallon, the Board (11-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to award Contract No.
    EP247-26 for Oxnard Accident Car and Out-Of-Service Car Rehabilitation, to SYSTRA
    Canada in the not-to-exceed amount of $21,021,924.16. This amount is to rehabilitate up to
    19 railcars that are currently long-term out-of-service due to sever accidents, obsolete parts,
    and/or degraded conditions from long out-of-service dwell times. The award is subject to
    resolution of any timely filed protests.

    The contract amount of $21,021,924.16 for this project is included in the FY23 and FY25
    Capital Budgets adopted by the SCRRA Board of Directors as well as reprogrammable
    capital budget for this specific project.

                                                                                                         802
                                                 13

7.H FY2025-26 Quarterly Fuel Purchase Program Update - Quarter Ending March 31, 2026

      Assistant Finance Director Alex Barber provided an update on the Authority's Fuel
      Purchase Program for the quarter ended March 31, 2025. As of March 31, 2026 the
      Authority’s hedging account had a value of $4,556,831, an increase of $2,182,218 from
      December 31, 2025. He explained with regard to global events affecting fuel prices,
      Metrolink is currently hedged out to November and is seeing benefits to those hedging
      contracts.

      Chair Chaffee asked if the increased fuel prices have led to an increase in ridership.

      Mr. Kettle stated it has been negligible.

      Director Marquez asked if hedging the fuel has been worth the time and effort over the years.

      Mr. Barber explained over the last six months staff has seen the gains from the fuel hedge
      have been extraordinary and are helping offset the price at the pump for a gallon of gas.
      When looking at the fuel hedge program, along with the purchasing of fuel, those two
      processes should really net to zero so as the fuel hedge is gaining money Metrolink is also
      paying more for the price of fuel so at the end of the day those two things should offset
      and remain flat.

      The Board received and filed this item.

7.I   May Legislative Update

      Government and Community Relations Director Jeff Dunn provided a monthly update on
      current legislative affairs. Staff participated in the annual CTA legislative conference in
      Sacramento and held meetings with senate and assembly offices of the Metrolink delegation
      to champion the agency’s funding request. He provided an update on the May revise and
      CARB’s draft auction market rules. He went over the Build America 250 Act and T-HUD
      appropriations.

      Director Spiegel asked about counties or commissions sending letters to support Metrolink by
      chiming in.

      Mr. Dunn confirmed there have been a few letters of support submitted by Board members
      and the template can be sent back out.

8.    Chief Executive Officer's Report

      Mr. Kettle shared Metrolink partnered with Bleecker Street Productions for a train wrap to
      advertise for an upcoming film. He touched on awards the agency received from SCAG and
      the California Transportation Foundation and a successful Bike Day. He announced the
      contactless payment pilot will launch in June on the San Bernardino line. He shared there
      will be special service for the World Cup and Deputy Chief Operating Officer Luis
      Carrasquero was recognized as one of Progressive Railroading’s 2026 Rising Stars. Mr.
      Kettle concluded with an update on the mechanical issues and shared the agency has made
      great progress on equipment reliability. He announced the June meeting will be moved up
      to 9:00 due to the LA Union Station Fan Fest.


                                                                                                      803
                                                  14

     Director Wapner noted when his train was running an hour late that they were allowing folks
     to ride for free and asked if it is typical.

     Mr. Kettle stated it is not typical and though nice, Metrolink needs fare revenue.

9.   Board Members' Comments – None.

10. Chair's Comments

     Chair Chaffee requested staff get the new virtual committee meeting set up as quickly as
     possible.

11. CONSENT CALENDAR

11.A Approval of Meeting Minutes - April 24, 2026 Regular Board Meeting

     The Board (11-0) approved the Minutes of the April 24, 2026 Regular Board Meeting.

11.B State Rail Assistance (SRA) Program Resolution

     The State of California's State Rail Assistance (SRA) Program requires that the Board
     adopt a resolution, provide required certifications and assurances, and delegate authority
     for execution of any actions necessary under this grant in order to receive SRA funds.

     The Board (11-0) adopted Resolution No. 26-150 Authorization for the Execution of the
     Resolution, Certifications and Assurances, and Authorized Agent Forms for the State Rail
     Assistance (SRA) Program to support the Fuel Efficiency and Maintenance Modernization

11.C Contract No. PO1046-26 - Railroad Track Materials - Recommendation to Award -
     Voestalpine Railway Systems Nortrak LLC

     The Authority requires track materials such as frogs, transition rail, and samson stock rail
     to support the continued maintenance and rehabilitation of its right-of-way system.

     The Board (11-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to award Contract No. PO1046-
     26 for the provision of Railroad Track Materials to Voestalpine Railway Systems Nortrak
     LLC in a not- to-exceed amount of $5,050,071 (including $351,232.58 to cover sales taxes)
     for a base term of two years, with a single one-year renewal option. The option may be
     exercised at the discretion of the CEO. This award is subject to the resolution of any timely
     submitted protest.

     The amount for which contract authority is requested is included in the proposed operating
     budget for FY27. Any use of these funds will be contingent upon the adoption of that
     budget. Funding for subsequent fiscal years will be requested through the annual budget
     process.




                                                                                                     804

11.D Contract C3169-26 - Train Wash Upgrade Project - Recommendation to Award - N/S
     Corporation

    The Authority requires repairs and upgrades to the Train Wash equipment at the Metrolink
    Central Maintenance Facility (CMF). The existing Train Wash system is not functioning
    properly and is currently not recycling water. As a result, it must be replaced to ensure
    safety, operational reliability, and sustainability.

    The Board (11-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to award Contract No. C3169-26

    The amounts for which contract authority is requesting are included in the adopted Capital

    This report presents an update on the Authority’s Accounts Receivable for the quarter

    The Board received and filed this report.

    The Authority’s Annual Investment Policy requires the Treasurer to make a quarterly

    SCRRA Working Capital Fund Policy - FIN 9.7, as well as executed Member Agency MOUs

TO:                       Board of Directors

FROM:                     Tom Schamber, Chief Financial Officer


SUBJECT:                  FY2026-27 Annual Contract Authority for Purchase of Various
                          Original Equipment Manufacturer Components, Information
                          Technology Products, Administrative and Operating Services,
                          Maintenance, Repair, and Operations Services, and Leases.


Issue

Annual authorization is required to continue the purchase of various Original Equipment
Manufacturer (OEM) components, Information Technology products, administrative and
operating services, maintenance, repair, and operations services, and leases.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the Board authorize the Chief Executive Officer to approve the contract
authority of the list of Annual items in Attachment A in a total not-to-exceed amount of
$28,894,801 for FY2026-27, and to extend the terms to June 30, 2027, contingent upon Board
approval of the FY2026-27 Operating Budget. The approval of contract authority does not
represent a commitment in the Budget, and purchases will be based on actual needs and
subject to budget availability.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Modernizing Business Practices: We will improve our operational efficiency through
      transparency, objective metrics and streamlined governance, reducing over-reliance on
      subsidy, while bringing our system into state of good repair and investing in the
      development of employees. These components and services support the
      Authority's business functions and system.



                                                                                                    821

Background

The Annuals Process has been a long-term practice for the Agency, and in past years, the
Annuals were part of the Budget Approval process.


The Authority began using the annual Board approval process in 2013 to seek annual
authority for five categories, including:

  1. Software License, Maintenance, and Support Agreements (Licenses)
  2. Original Equipment Manufacturers Agreements for Rolling Stock Components,
     Communication Signal Equipment, and Positive Train Control Requirements (OEMs)
  3. Maintenance, Repair and Operations Agreements (MROs)
  4. Administrative and Operating Services Agreements (Admin & Ops)
  5. Communication Network Towers and Related Leasing Agreements (Towers)

As part of the Annuals development process, staff assessed the services and agreements
included in Attachment A to ensure compliance with the Procurement and Contracting
Policies, last modified on April 1, 2026. The requested annual authority for the agreements
listed in Attachment A is based on estimates developed by the respective Project Managers
as part of the FY2026-27 budget development process. This year, since budget adoption was
deferred, the Annuals are being requested separately.


Discussion

Authorization is required for the annual agreements listed below:

Software License, Maintenance, and Support Agreements (Licenses)
Annual license and support renewals for various required software packages and services to
continue Authority operations, including the network, financial system, asset management,
train scheduling, safety management, Computer Aided Dispatch system, and Positive Train
Control (PTC). The PTC software in use is proprietary and requires licenses, subscriptions,
and/or support agreements with the manufacturer or designated distributor.

Original Equipment Manufacturers Agreements for Rolling Stock Components,
Communication Signal Equipment, and Positive Train Control Requirements (OEMs)
Purchase components and parts to continue the maintenance and rehabilitation of the
Authority's rolling stock components and fulfill track and communication, signal, and Positive
Train Control requirements.

Maintenance, Repair, and Operations (MRO) Agreements
These agreements are for goods, services, and materials, to support facility maintenance and
operations - the goods and services being purchased under these agreements consist of
routine shop supplies required to support maintenance and repair work.

Administrative and Operating Services Agreements (Admin & Ops)
These administrative and operating agreements support the Authority's business functions
and system.

                                                                                                 822

Communication Network Towers and Related Leasing Agreements (Towers)
The Authority requires communication tower lease agreements within the Authority's right-of-
way and at strategic remote locations to support Train Control Systems, including Positive
Train Control (PTC) and the Authority's communication network.


Budget Impact

The amounts for which annual authority is requested are included in, and contingent upon, the
adoption of the Proposed FY2026-27 Operating Budget. For the period July 1, 2026 through
September 30, 2026 funds will be provided by the FY27 Continuing Appropriations Resolution,
and contingent upon its approval.


Next Steps

Upon approval by the Board, staff will issue as-needed purchase orders based on actual
needs and subject to budget availability.

ITEM ID:                   2026-248-0

MEETING DATE:              June 26, 2026

TO:                        Board of Directors

FROM:                      Paul Hubler, Chief Strategy Officer


SUBJECT:                   Rail-2-Rail Agreement - Time Extension No. 9


Issue

The current Rail-2-Rail (R2R) Agreement with the Los Angeles - San Diego - San Luis Obispo
Rail Corridor Agency (LOSSAN) and the National Passenger Railroad Corporation (Amtrak)
was last extended to June 30, 2026. An amendment to the agreement is needed to continue
the program past June 30, 2026.

Usage of the R2R program has also increased significantly in the last year. Since the program
is paid for on a per-passenger basis, the cost of the program has also increased. This requires
an amendment to increase contract authority.


Recommendation

It is recommended that the Board authorize the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and
execute an amendment which extends Agreement No. L-9-0005 between LOSSAN, the
Southern California Regional Rail Authority (Authority), and Amtrak to continue the Rail-2-Rail
(R2R) program for up to a six-month term through December 31, 2026, and increase the total
maximum contract value to $6,708,887.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Connecting and Leveraging Partnerships: We will forge new and enhanced
      relationships with our public and private partners to integrate and coordinate connecting
      services, providing residents throughout Southern California with better, seamless,



                                                                                                     831

     sustainable alternatives to driving. This agreement advances a partnership between the
     Authority, LOSSAN, and Amtrak which creates opportunities for reciprocal travel that is
     greater than each of their separate services.


Background

The R2R program was initiated in 2003 through a cooperative agreement between the
California Department of Transportation (Caltrans), the Authority, and Amtrak. The R2R
program was intended to leverage available capacity on the Pacific Surfliner for the mutual
benefit of both the Authority and the Pacific Surfliner by providing additional capacity for
Metrolink passengers at a time when the Authority needed capacity and had no options to
provide it. The program also intended to help increase ridership and fare revenue on the
Pacific Surfliner by carrying Metrolink passengers. The more prominent expression of R2R is
a mutual pass acceptance between the Pacific Surfliner and Metrolink on the lines that follow
the LOSSAN Corridor – the Orange County Line, the Ventura County Line, and portions of the
Antelope Valley Line, 91/Perris Valley Line, and IEOC Line that share stations with those lines.
R2R allows Pacific Surfliner and Metrolink monthly passholders to utilize either service within
the limits of their valid ticket at no additional charge and provides for a reciprocal use for
Pacific Surfliner passengers.

Currently, the R2R program allows the Authority to offer up to 24 additional daily trips to its
monthly passholders at a fraction of the cost to provide that service independently. A
secondary expression of the R2R Program is the concept of shared services or "codeshare."
With the codeshare concept, certain trips of the Pacific Surfliner operate as if they are also
Metrolink trains. They are included on the Metrolink schedule and accept all Metrolink fare
media to ride. This type of arrangement was initiated in 2005 and applied to one trip in each
direction on the portion of the LOSSAN corridor between Los Angeles Union Station and
Ventura County (parallel to the Ventura County Line), under the name “Shared Services.” In
October 2021, this was extended to a second roundtrip and renamed "Codeshare" to improve
passenger understanding because codeshare trains are effectively treated as part of the
Metrolink schedule. In both cases, shared services or codeshare was implemented because
Metrolink relinquished schedule slots it operated in so that the Pacific Surfliner could schedule
trains in those slots. Codeshare allowed Metrolink and its passengers to be kept whole while
still accommodating Amtrak's desire to implement their new schedules.

On March 18, 2019, the LOSSAN Board of Directors approved Cooperative Agreement L-9-
0005, which extended the R2R Program between the Authority and Amtrak for a term of one
year through June 30, 2020, at $7 per boarding. It has since been extended by amendment
eight times, now ending June 30, 2026.

On November 1, 2023, a pilot program to expand code share to apply to all Surfliner trains
between Los Angeles and Ventura-Downtown/Beach Station was implemented to be in effect
until June 30, 2025, and the reimbursement rate, for codeshare boardings only, was increased
to $10. This has also been extended by amendments and now also ends June 30, 2026.


Discussion

The Authority and LOSSAN have continued to discuss the code share pilot program and R2R

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit



                              EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The Internal Audit Department (Internal Audit) completed the Audit of Inventory
Obsolescence Controls (Project No. 2026-04-IA) as part of the Board approved Fiscal
Year 2026 Annual Internal Audit Plan.

SCRRA maintains railroad operating spare parts inventory consisting primarily of
Mechanical, Communications and Signal, and Track and Structure materials used to
support rolling stock maintenance, signal system reliability, and right-of-way
infrastructure. Materials Management is responsible for purchasing, controlling, and
monitoring this inventory in coordination with operating departments and maintenance
contractors. As of February 28, 2026, SCRRA maintained approximately $33.2 million in
inventory across 13 inventory locations and 5 right-of-way locations along the rail system.

Objective:

The objective of this audit was to evaluate whether SCRRA has established adequate
procedures, processes, and internal controls to identify, monitor, and manage obsolete,
excess, or inactive inventory in a timely manner.

Scope Limitation:

The following scope limitations were identified during the audit:

 Inventory associated with the Arrow fleet was excluded from the scope of this audit
  because it is not managed within SCRRA’s inventory systems.
 Parts management and maintenance planning activities related to the overall
  locomotive fleet, including funding, parts availability, and supply chain constraints
  impacting maintenance activities and procurement of materials, were outside the
  scope of this audit and were not reviewed in detail.

Findings and Recommendations:

Findings:
   1. End-to-End Process for Managing Obsolete Inventory Not Fully Documented
   2. Current Inventory System Capabilities Are Limited
   3. Opportunities Exist to Improve Monitoring of Long-Inactive Inventory
Recommendations:
  1. Develop and document a comprehensive end-to-end procedure for managing
     obsolete inventory across its full lifecycle
  2. Evaluate opportunities to enhance system functionality and processes to better
     support forecasting and inventory planning
  3. Strengthen inventory monitoring and tracking practices, including documentation
     of inventory adjustments, visibility over materials outside the inventory system, and
     classification of inactive inventory

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit



                                       INTRODUCTION

The Internal Audit Department conducted an audit of Inventory Obsolescence Controls
(Project No. 2026-04-IA). This audit was included in the Fiscal Year 2026 Annual Internal
Audit Plan approved by the Board of Directors.

                                        BACKGROUND

SCRRA maintains inventory consisting of railroad operating spare parts that support
rolling stock maintenance, communications and signal systems, and track and structure
infrastructure. Materials Management (MM) is responsible for the purchasing, control, and
monitoring of this inventory and supports rolling stock, track, and signals and
communications maintenance activities. Materials Management coordinates with
operating departments and maintenance contractors to support equipment maintenance,
right-of-way repair, and signal system reliability.

Materials Management reviews inventory usage to identify inactive or outdated items and
maintain warehouse space for critical parts. Maintaining accurate inventory records also
supports accurate financial reporting. Without timely review and disposition, obsolete
inventory may accumulate and create financial and operational risk.

SCRRA maintains three primary inventory types: Mechanical Inventory, Communications
and Signal Inventory, and Track and Structure Inventory. These categories support
locomotive and railcar maintenance, signal and communication system reliability, and
right-of-way infrastructure repair and maintenance. As of February 28, 2026, Materials
Management oversees these inventory categories with a total balance of $33,235,409,
stored across 13 inventory locations (including maintenance facilities and storage yards)
and five right-of-way locations along the rail system.

The table below summarizes inventory balances by inventory type as of February 28,
2026.


                          Inventory Type              Balance at 2/28/2026*
                    Mechanical Inventory                      $ 18,834,017
                    Track & Structure                             7,776,966
                    Communications & Signal                       6,624,426
                    Total                                     $ 33,235,409
* Information obtained from a report generated by Materials Management Department entitled “Inventory
Locations 2/28/2026”

Materials Management maintains Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and financial
policies that govern inventory management, including procedures related to inventory
monitoring, review of inactive inventory, and financial accounting for inventory
adjustments.


                                                  1
                                                                                                        921

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit


Inventory transactions and balances are recorded in the Trapeze Enterprise Asset
Management (Trapeze) system, which serves as the operational system of record for
asset maintenance and inventory activity. The system is used to track inventory
quantities, record receipts and issuances, and support maintenance operations across
rolling stock, track infrastructure, and signal systems.

SCRRA contracted with Trapeze Software Group in November 2020 to implement an
Enterprise Asset Management system to support a centralized asset management
environment. The system is intended to consolidate previously siloed asset management
functions and support improved monitoring, reporting, and management of agency
assets.

The Financial Information System (FIS) is used for financial reporting and general ledger
activity. Inventory balances recorded in the Trapeze system are reconciled to the general
ledger within FIS to support financial reporting.

                 OBJECTIVES, SCOPE, AND METHODOLOGY

                                      OBJECTIVES
The objective of this audit was to evaluate whether SCRRA has established adequate
procedures, processes, and internal controls to identify, monitor, and manage obsolete,
excess, or inactive inventory in a timely manner.

                                          SCOPE
The scope of this audit included inventory balances, activity, and related monitoring
controls for the period January 1, 2025, through February 28, 2026. The audit focused
on how SCRRA identifies inactive or obsolete inventory, reviews and approves
disposition, and records related financial adjustments. Audit procedures included
reviewing inventory data in the Trapeze system. Audit procedures excluded reviewing
accounting treatment, financial reporting, and general ledger activities within the
Financial Information System (FIS).

Scope Limitations and Out-of-Scope Matters

Inventory associated with the Arrow fleet was excluded from this audit because it is not
managed within SCRRA’s inventory systems.

In addition, during the audit, Internal Audit identified several high-risk concerns related to
parts management and maintenance planning for the overall locomotive fleet. These
concerns reflect broader challenges for the Agency.

Based on discussions with management and review of March 27, 2026, Board of
Directors Meeting materials, funding constraints have limited the consistent performance
of scheduled maintenance and major engine overhauls, contributing to component
failures. These issues are further exacerbated by the Agency being the sole operator of


                                              2
                                                                                                 922

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit


the F125 locomotive, which has created significant procurement hurdles due to the
extremely limited production of parts and lack of a broader market for the equipment.
Furthermore, general supply chain constraints (such as long lead times for parts and
limited availability of components sourced internationally) have hindered the timely
acquisition of materials. Collectively, these factors have contributed to recent service
reductions implemented by the Agency.

While these matters may impact inventory planning and operations, they were outside the
scope of this audit and were not reviewed in detail.

                                    METHODOLOGY
To accomplish the audit objective, Internal Audit:

   Interviewed key personnel within Materials Management, Operations, Program
    Delivery, and Finance.

   Reviewed relevant policies and Standard Operating Procedures related to inventory
    monitoring and disposition.

   Obtained and analyzed inventory activity reports out of the Trapeze System.

   Performed data analysis of inventory activity reports to identify long-inactive
    inventory items and locations with higher concentrations of excess or obsolete
    inventory.

   Conducted site visits and inventory observations at selected inventory locations to
    assess inventory condition, storage practices, and the presence of inactive or
    obsolete materials.

   Evaluated the design and operating effectiveness of controls related to the
    identification, review, approval, and disposition of obsolete inventory, including
    coordination between Materials Management, Operations, and Finance.

   Reviewed supporting documentation for selected inventory items to assess
    compliance with established procedures.
We conducted this performance audit in accordance with generally accepted government
auditing standards and in conformance with the Global Internal Audit Standards
promulgated by the Institute of Internal Auditors. Those standards require that we plan
and perform the audit to obtain sufficient and appropriate evidence to provide a
reasonable basis for our findings and conclusions based on our audit objectives. We
believe that the evidence obtained provides a reasonable basis for our findings and
conclusions based on our audit objectives.

                                      CONCLUSION
Overall, Internal Audit found that SCRRA has established processes to monitor inventory
activity and identify inventory that may be inactive or obsolete. Materials Management


                                              3
                                                                                           923

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit


performs periodic reviews of inventory usage and coordinates with Operations and
Finance when inventory items are identified for potential disposition, demonstrating a
proactive approach to inventory oversight.

While these processes provide a foundation for monitoring inventory activity,
opportunities exist to improve documentation of the obsolete inventory process,
strengthen system capabilities, improve inventory data completeness, and enhance
monitoring of long-inactive inventory. Addressing these areas will help improve visibility
over inventory and support more consistent identification and disposition of obsolete
materials.




                                             4
                                                                                             924

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit


       OBSERVATIONS, RECOMMENDATIONS, AND MANAGEMENT
                         RESPONSES

Finding 1: End-to-End Process for Managing Obsolete Inventory Not Fully
Documented
Criteria

The May 2025 Standards for Internal Control in the Federal Government (Green Book),
issued by the U.S. Government Accountability Office, establish that internal control should
be designed and implemented to help management achieve objectives and respond to
risks.

      Section 1 Fundamental Concepts of Internal Control Section OV1.01 states
       “Internal control is a process effected by an entity’s oversight body, management,
       and other personnel, designed to provide reasonable assurance that the objectives
       of an entity will be achieved.”
      Section 1 Fundamental Concepts of Internal Controls Section OV1.04 states
       “Control activities are actions that management establishes through policies and
       procedures as part of the control activities component to specifically mitigate risks
       to achieving the entity’s objectives to acceptable levels.”
Condition

SCRRA does not have a single documented end-to-end procedure for identifying,
reviewing, approving, and disposing of obsolete inventory.

As part of the audit, Internal Audit reviewed inventory-related Standard Operating
Procedures (SOPs) and policies to determine whether SCRRA has documented
procedures for identifying, reviewing, approving, and disposing of obsolete inventory. The
following documents were reviewed:

      SOP MM-01 – Materials Management
      SOP MM-02 – Inventory Management
      SOP MM-03 – Vendor Managed Inventory (VMI)
      SOP MM-04 – Storeroom After-Hours Access
      SOP MM-05 – Repair and Return
      SOP MM-06 – Contractor Materials Process:
      Finance Policy FIN -4.5 -Railroad Parts/Materials Inventory Recovery

Based on Internal Audit’s review, SOP MM-02 – Inventory Management and Finance
Policy FIN-4.5 – Railroad Parts / Materials Inventory Recovery address certain aspects
of the obsolete inventory process. SOP MM-02 includes criteria for identifying obsolete
inventory and elements of the review and approval process, while Finance Policy FIN-4.5
addresses the accounting treatment of obsolete inventory, including identification, write-



                                             5
                                                                                               925

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit


offs/downs, and financial reporting. However, these documents do not provide a
complete description of the full lifecycle or reflect a comprehensive, end-to-end workflow.

A complete lifecycle would include documented procedures describing how each of the
following steps are performed:
     How items are identified as obsolete, including criteria and responsible personnel
     Who is responsible for notifying appropriate personnel and how that notification
       occurs
     What documentation is required to support disposition decisions and how it is
       maintained
     How approvals are obtained, including required levels of approval and Member
       Agency concurrence where applicable
     How the method of disposal is determined (e.g., auction, sale, donation, or
       discard)
     How disposal activities are executed, including roles and responsibilities
     How proceeds are transferred to Finance
     How inventory is removed or adjusted within the Trapeze system.
Cause

The obsolete inventory review and disposition process has developed over time through
operational practices across multiple departments and has not been consolidated into a
single documented end-to-end procedure.
Effect

The risk of not having a documented end-to-end process for managing obsolete inventory
is that inventory review, disposition, and tracking activities may be performed
inconsistently, limiting management oversight and clarity for staff responsible for these
activities.
Recommendation

   1. Materials Management should develop and document a single, comprehensive
      end-to-end procedure that describes the full lifecycle for managing obsolete
      inventory. The procedure should define how each step in the process is performed,
      including:

            How items are identified as obsolete, including criteria and responsible
             personnel.
            Who is responsible for notifying appropriate personnel and how that notification
             occurs.
            What documentation is required to support disposition decisions and how it is
             maintained.
            How approvals are obtained, including required levels of approval and Member
             Agency concurrence where applicable.



                                               6
                                                                                                926

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit


          How the method of disposal is determined (e.g., auction, sale, donation, or
           discard).
          How disposal activities are executed, including roles and responsibilities.
          How proceeds are transferred to Finance and recorded.
          How inventory is removed or adjusted within the Trapeze System, including
           supporting documentation for inventory adjustments and disposals.

       Management Response

       Management agrees. While aspects of inventory obsolescence processes are
       captured in various SOPs, a single, comprehensive SOP would be more
       effective.

       Corrective Action Plan

       1. A comprehensive inventory obsolescence SOP will be developed and
          implemented.

       Target Implementation Date

       October 31, 2026

       Responsible for Implementation

       Cynthia Minix, Director of CPMM
       Eduardo Tovar, Manager II Inventory Control
       Accountable for Implementation
       Tom Schamber, Chief Financial Officer

Finding 2: Current Inventory System Capabilities Are Limited
Criteria

The May 2025 Standards for Internal Control in the Federal Government (Green Book),
issued by the U.S. Government Accountability Office, provide criteria for designing,
implementing, and operating effective internal control systems. The following Green Book
criteria were applicable:

   •   Section 1: Fundamental Concepts of Internal Control, OV1.03 states: “Internal
       control comprises the plans, methods, policies, procedures, and other
       mechanisms used to fulfill the mission, strategic plan, goals, and objectives of the
       entity.”
   •   Principle 13 – Use Quality Information indicates that management should use
       quality information to achieve the entity’s objectives. This principle further



                                             7
                                                                                              927

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit


       indicates that relevant data from reliable sources should be processed into quality
       information to support internal control and operational decision-making.

Condition

SCRRA utilizes the Trapeze system to manage inventory quantities and record inventory
transactions. The system supports key inventory functions, including tracking quantities
on hand, recording receipts and issuances, and maintaining inventory records across
multiple locations.

However, based on discussions with Materials Management personnel and review of
system reports, the current system configuration provides limited support in certain areas
that assist with inventory monitoring and planning. As a result, some activities such as
inventory aging analysis and forecasting require manual analysis outside of the system
using reports and spreadsheets.

Examples of system limitations noted during the audit include:

•   Limited forecasting functionality.
    Based on discussions with Materials Management personnel and review of system
    functionality, the Trapeze system does not currently provide robust tools to support
    forecasting future inventory demand. As a result, forecasting and planning activities
    rely in part on manual analysis and operational knowledge.
•   Limited ability to generate extended aging analysis.
    Management generates reports identifying items with no activity for five years as part
    of its process to review inventory that may be classified as excess or obsolete and
    submits to Applicable Project Managers for evaluation. Determining the age of
    inventory items requires manual review and analysis of the underlying data. During
    audit procedures, Internal Audit expanded this analysis to identify inventory with no
    activity for ten or more years using external data analysis. The current system does
    not readily produce summary aging reports with defined aging categories, which may
    make it more difficult to quickly identify long-inactive inventory.
•   Limited ability to evaluate operational needs for inactive inventory.
    During inventory observations, Internal Audit noted that certain Track & Structure and
    Signals & Communications components had no activity for more than ten years but
    may still be required due to long lead times or specialized infrastructure needs. In
    some cases, these items may have significant replacement costs. The current system
    does not allow management to flag or classify these items to indicate that they remain
    operationally necessary despite long periods of inactivity.
•   Limited linkage between inventory and underlying assets.




                                             8
                                                                                             928

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit


    Effective forecasting may require the ability to link inventory items to the assets they
    support (e.g., rolling stock, track infrastructure, or signal and communication
    systems). Currently, this linkage does not exist in the current system. Without this
    linkage, it may be more difficult to determine whether certain inventory items are still
    required when related assets are retired, replaced, or upgraded.

Cause

The Trapeze system is primarily configured to support asset, maintenance, and inventory
transaction tracking. Certain analytical capabilities related to inventory monitoring,
forecasting, and lifecycle analysis are limited within the current system functionality. As a
result, some inventory management activities have developed over time through manual
analysis and operational practices outside of the system.

Effect

The risk of limited system capabilities for inventory management is that certain inventory
monitoring and planning activities may rely on manual processes, which may reduce
efficiency and limit management visibility over inventory activity and planning needs.

   Recommendation

     2. Materials Management, in coordination with Information Technology, should
        evaluate whether system enhancements or upgrades to the Trapeze system are
        available to improve inventory monitoring and planning capabilities, including
        aging analysis, demand forecasting, useful life tracking, and linkage between
        inventory items and related assets.

   Management Response

   Management agrees. Trapeze functionality for forecasting is extremely limited, and
   manual processes using spreadsheets are ineffective and inefficient.

   Corrective Action Plan

   2. A dedicated forecasting software solution will be identified and implemented
      subject to budgetary constraints.

   Target Implementation Date

   December 31, 2027

   Responsible for Implementation

   Cynthia Minix, Director of CPMM
   Eduardo Tovar, Manager II Inventory Control



                                             9
                                                                                                929

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit


     Accountable for Implementation
     Tom Schamber, Chief Financial Officer

Finding 3: Opportunities Exist to Improve Monitoring of Long-Inactive
Inventory

Criteria

The May 2025 Standards for Internal Control in the Federal Government (Green Book),
issued by the U.S. Government Accountability Office, provide criteria for designing,
implementing, and operating effective internal control systems. The following Green Book
criteria were applicable:

     •    Principle 10: Design Control Activities indicate that management should design
          control activities to achieve objectives and respond to risks.
     •    Principle 12: Implement Control Activities indicates that management should
          implement control activities through policies and procedures that establish
          responsibilities and documentation requirements.

Condition

During the audit, Internal Audit obtained information from Materials Management
identifying inventory that had no receipt or issuance activity for 10 or more years. The
information provided by Materials Management was as of February 28, 2026, and
reflected inventory items with no activity (receipts or issuances) during the previous 10
years.

As of this date, SCRRA maintained approximately $33.2* million in total inventory. Of
this amount, approximately $3,364,835 represented inventory items that had no activity
for more than 10 years, as summarized below.

Based on this information, Internal Audit selected the three locations with the highest
dollar values within each inventory category to perform site visits and physically observe
inventory items that had no activity for more than 10 years. The locations observed
represented approximately 63 percent of the total inventory value identified with no
activity during this period.

                                         Total 10+ Year
 Inventory Type                          Inactive Inventory**             Location Observed                    Value Tested
 Signal & Communications                           $ 1,091,711            Melbourne – Pomona                       $ 1,051,265
 Equipment                                           1,063,598            CMF – Los Angeles                            427,013
 Track & Structure                                   1,209,526            Lang – Canyon Country                        639,118
 Total                                             $ 3,364,835                                                     $ 2,117,396

* Information obtained from a report generated by Materials Management Department entitled “Inventory Locations 2/28/2026”
** Information obtained from a report generated by Materials Management Department that reflects inactive inventory for 10 or more
years as of February 28, 2026.




                                                               10
                                                                                                                                     930

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit



Internal Audit conducted site visits at each of the locations listed above and performed
test counts of selected inventory items with no activity for more than 10 years. Procedures
also included observation of storage conditions and discussions with inventory personnel
regarding the operational need for these items. Test counts confirmed that the items
reviewed were generally present and identifiable; however, several observations were
noted regarding how long-inactive inventory is monitored, classified, and stored.

   Inventory write-off without documented approval
    Internal Audit identified a Track and Structure component (Part ID 01-3434660-2 –
    turnout assembly for 136-lb rail) that was written off in the Trapeze inventory system
    on November 4, 2025. Yard personnel indicated the decision was discussed verbally
    with management; however, written approval documentation was not on hand at the
    time of review.

   Certain project-related and scrap materials are not recorded in Trapeze
    Internal Audit noted that certain materials stored at field locations are not recorded in
    the Trapeze inventory system. These materials primarily include items associated with
    capital projects, such as unused project materials and components removed from the
    rail system and retained for potential reuse, as well as scrap materials (e.g., concrete
    ties and crossing panels). Because these items were not purchased through the
    inventory system, they are tracked separately (e.g., spreadsheets) and are not
    reflected in Trapeze inventory records. Management also noted that some of these
    materials are large and difficult to remove, as disposal would require hauling and
    associated costs.

   Long-inactive inventory may not be properly classified
    During the Melbourne warehouse site visit, it was noted that some items identified as
    having no receipt or issuance activity for 10 or more years are still needed for
    operations. As discussed in Finding 2, The current system does not allow
    management to flag or classify these items to indicate that they remain operationally
    necessary despite long periods of inactivity.
Cause

Procedures for documenting inventory write-offs, recording materials returned from
projects, and managing scrap materials at field locations are not clearly defined or
consistently applied.
Effect

Without clear procedures and documentation requirements, inventory adjustments may
not be fully reflected in financial records, materials stored at field locations may not be
captured in inventory records or project accounting, and scrap materials may occupy
storage space that could otherwise be used for active inventory.

TO:                       Board of Directors

FROM:                     Justin Fornelli, Chief, Program Delivery


SUBJECT:                  Capital Program Status Report


Issue

Staff is providing an update on the progress of the Authority’s Capital Program, including the
Southern California Optimized Rail Expansion (SCORE) Program and the State of Good
Repair Program.

Recommendation

Receive and file.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Modernizing Business Practices: We will improve our operational efficiency through
      transparency, objective metrics and streamlined governance, reducing over-reliance on
      subsidy while bringing our system into a state of good repair and investing in the
      development of our employees. The report provides our Board with timely updates on
      the progress of the Capital Program. The new capital program, including SCORE, adds
      to the safety, expansion, and growth of the system while the State of Good Repair
      Program ensures the safety and reliability of the Authority’s existing assets.


Background

The Capital Program consists of two major components: New Capital Projects and State of
Good Repair (SoGR) Programs. The Authority’s Capital Program, outside of SCORE, is



                                                                                                    937

budgeted annually, and projects are typically delivered over multiple years. Funding for capital
projects is provided by Member Agencies through the annual budget process. The Authority
also applies for local, state, and federal funds for additional SoGR and New Capital Projects.

New Capital Projects expand railroad infrastructure and improve customer experience,
including items such as new sidings, safety enhancements to grade crossings, modernizing
signal and communication systems, and new rolling stock.

The SoGR Program addresses existing capital assets to keep them in a state of good repair
through activities such as:
     Rehabilitation of tunnels, bridges, and culverts
     Replacement of worn ties and rail
     Replacement of worn or outdated signal system components
     Programmed rehabilitation of rolling stock components such as car door operators and
     heating/ventilation/air conditioning (HVAC), and mid-life overhaul of rail cars and
     locomotives

All project progress is tracked through the Authority’s project reporting system, which is
maintained by the Program Management Oversight (PMO) department. Regular meetings are
held with project managers to review the progress of active projects. Staff also prepare
quarterly project expenditure forecasts to estimate cash flow requirements.

As part of the PMO’s effort to improve its reporting and tracking capabilities, key performance
indicators (KPIs) have been developed and are included in this report. This item has been
updated to reflect financial expenditure and project status through March 31, 2026.


Discussion


Since the last Capital Program Status Update in April 2026, multiple key accomplishments
were achieved, as follows:

SCORE Program:

     Received construction bids for the Marengo Siding Extension and Rancho Cucamonga
     Siding Extension projects on the San Gabriel Sub. The team is reviewing the proposals.
     The process of environmental clearance on Fullerton Interlocker has been started with 30% design.
     Continuing negotiations with the City of El Monte on the Purchase & Sale Agreement on the El Mont
     Started design process on the Lilac to Sycamore Double Track Project
     Started preliminary engineering on the Control Point Riverside 2nd Crossover Project
     Starting procurement of design consultant for Katherine and Tampa crossing on the Ventura Sub.
     Continuing negotiations with Union Pacific over the fiber relocation issue for the Simi Valley Double T



Authority staff have been collaborating with our funding partners at CalSTA, Caltrans, and the
Member Agencies to determine strategies to address projected funding gaps and advance key
projects. These strategies include prioritizing projects based on operational benefits,
reallocation of available funds from projects that have been completed under budget or that


                                                                                                   938

have been deferred and pursuing additional grant funding opportunities. Authority has also
been conducting a robust risk analysis and assessment of the costs associated with labor and
material to find efficiencies. Specifically, the Authority is working with Metro to pursue $206M
funding to bridge some of the gaps for projects on the Antelope Valley Line.


State of Good Repair Program:

     On-Board Train Control Systems Rehabilitation:
         Train Management Computer Upgrade: 132 out of 140 units have been upgraded.
         Estimate time of completion to upgrade remaining units is December 2026. Due to
         this being an industry-wide upgrade, the vendor is experiencing parts shortages

      Modernizing Business Practices: SCRRA will continue improving operational

      internal controls and oversight processes. Through this audit, opportunities for
      improvement were identified related to inventory obsolescence policies, system
      functionality, inventory tracking, and monitoring practices to support more effective
      inventory management operations.

2026-04-IA – Inventory Obsolescence Controls Audit



                              EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The Internal Audit Department (Internal Audit) completed the Audit of Inventory
Obsolescence Controls (Project No. 2026-04-IA) as part of the Board approved Fiscal
Year 2026 Annual Internal Audit Plan.

SCRRA maintains railroad operating spare parts inventory consisting primarily of
Mechanical, Communications and Signal, and Track and Structure materials used to
support rolling stock maintenance, signal system reliability, and right-of-way
infrastructure. Materials Management is responsible for purchasing, controlling, and
monitoring this inventory in coordination with operating departments and maintenance
contractors. As of February 28, 2026, SCRRA maintained approximately $33.2 million in
inventory across 13 inventory locations and 5 right-of-way locations along the rail system.

Objective:

The objective of this audit was to evaluate whether SCRRA has established adequate
procedures, processes, and internal controls to identify, monitor, and manage obsolete,
excess, or inactive inventory in a timely manner.

Scope Limitation:

The following scope limitations were identified during the audit:

 Inventory associated with the Arrow fleet was excluded from the scope of this audit
  because it is not managed within SCRRA’s inventory systems.
 Parts management and maintenance planning activities related to the overall
  locomotive fleet, including funding, parts availability, and supply chain constraints
  impacting maintenance activities and procurement of materials, were outside the
  scope of this audit and were not reviewed in detail.

Findings and Recommendations:

Findings:
   1. End-to-End Process for Managing Obsolete Inventory Not Fully Documented
   2. Current Inventory System Capabilities Are Limited
   3. Opportunities Exist to Improve Monitoring of Long-Inactive Inventory
Recommendations:
  1. Develop and document a comprehensive end-to-end procedure for managing
     obsolete inventory across its full lifecycle
  2. Evaluate opportunities to enhance system functionality and processes to better
     support forecasting and inventory planning
  3. Strengthen inventory monitoring and tracking practices, including documentation
     of inventory adjustments, visibility over materials outside the inventory system, and
     classification of inactive inventory
