Section 7.           Unsolicited Proposals

An Unsolicited Proposal is a written proposal that is submitted to the Authority on the initiative of
the submitter that is not a response to a formal or informal request issued by the Authority. It must
have the following qualities:

          •   Innovative and unique;

          •   Independently originated and developed by the proposer;

          •   Of sufficient size and benefit to potentially warrant a full review process by the Authority;
          •   Prepared without the Authority's supervision, endorsement, direction, or direct
              involvement; and

          •   Sufficiently detailed that its benefits in support of the Authority's mission and
              responsibilities are apparent.

The Authority may award a contract in response to an unsolicited proposal if permitted by
applicable law, and if the proposal presents an innovative and unique opportunity and is
independently originated and developed by the offerors without Authority participation. The
Authority does not commit to any particular outcome (including that Authority engagement with
the proposer will lead to a procurement or a contract with the proposer). All costs incurred by a
proposer in discussing an Unsolicited Proposal with the Authority, in preparing any materials, and
in any way engaging with the Authority regarding an Unsolicited Proposal will be borne solely
and completely by the proposer.

Section 8.           Procurement Solicitation and Award

A.            Independent Cost Estimate

Prior to commencing a procurement, the department or division requesting the procurement will
prepare an independent cost estimate for every procurement valued over $150,000. An independent
cost estimate is not required for micro-purchases.

B.            Solicitation Documents

Solicitations may not be drafted in a manner that limits bidding or proposing unnecessarily or
intentionally to any one offeror, nor may solicitations be split to avoid the need for full and open
competition or to avoid adhering to a federal or state law or regulation, or Authority policy.

     i.       Formal competitive bidding requires preparation of bid documents that clearly set forth all
              requirements, which must be fulfilled in order for the bid to be responsive, and must be
              advertised in accordance with legal requirements. An award, if made, will be to the lowest
              responsive and responsible bidder.

                                                       10

                                                                                                              34

 ii.   Formal competitive proposals, such as the "best value" approach, require issuance of
       Requests for Proposals, which clearly set forth all the requirements, and state the qualitative
       factors in addition to price, which will be used to evaluate and rank the Proposals. An
       award, if made, will be to the proposer receiving the highest ranking, subject to successful
       negotiations with the Authority.

If a contract will be federally-funded, all relevant federal provisions must be included in the
solicitation documents.

C.     Advertising

Advertising regarding a procurement must comply with applicable federal and state laws,
regulations and requirements.

D.     Bonds

All public works procurements must comply with federal, state, and local requirements concerning
bonds and securities. Non-public work procurements may require bonds and securities when
determined to be in the best interest of the Authority and legal counsel concurs. If bonds are
required, the solicitation documents must specify the required items and their values.

E.     Contingency Fund

A contingency fund may be established by the Board to provide additional contract funding
authorization when there is a likelihood that unknown conditions or circumstances may occur
during the term of a contract that necessitates an increase in the contractor’s compensation.

F.     Fair and Reasonable Determination

For every procurement action, including change orders and contract amendments, the Authority
must determine that prices to be paid are fair and reasonable. The Contracts and Procurement
Department will have final responsibility for accepting or making such a determination. The
analysis must be kept with the procurement record.

G.     Contract Award

Any and all bids or proposals may be rejected by the Authority if it is in the Authority's best interest
to do so.

The Authority may only contract with contractors who are trustworthy and are qualified and
possess the ability to perform successfully under the terms and conditions of the proposed
procurement.

Unsuccessful proposers/bidders may request a debrief after the contract is awarded.

Section 9.     Protests

A protest may be filed for contracts in excess of $25,000 only by an Interested Party, defined

applicable protest deadlines will be provided in all formal solicitations. To be considered, a
protest must be filed in a timely manner and must satisfy all of the applicable requirements set

Except pursuant to statutory rules requiring Board determination of protests of contracts for

Section 13. Small Business Partnership Program Policy

In order to provide economic opportunity for small businesses, and to stimulate economic
development in communities served by the Southern California Regional Rail Authority
(Authority), it is the policy of the Authority to ensure that small business enterprises (SBEs), as
defined by the Small Business Administration and local small business enterprises with a
principal office within the Authority’s six-county service area, have equitable opportunity to
participate in the agency’s procurement of all goods, materials and services.

   1. To ensure nondiscrimination in the award and administration of non-federally funded

   2. To create a level playing field on which SBEs can compete fairly for non-federally funded
      contracts;

   3. To ensure that firms fully meet certified eligibility standards as determined by federal,
      state, or local agencies, or an agreed upon, third-party certifying entity;

   4. To expand business building opportunities by establishing specific and distinct business
      building opportunities for SBEs participating in non-federally funded contracts;

   5. To help remove barriers to the participation of SBEs in non-federally funded contracts.
      Barriers to be removed may include but not be limited to adjusting contract requirements
      related to bonding and insurance requirements;

   6. To support improved cash flow for SBEs by documenting prompt payment terms; and

   7. To provide local small businesses non-federally funded contract incentives such as set aside
      programs and local preference points. The Authority will apply five (5) local preference
      points to the score of a response to a procurement received from a local small business that
      is designated as Contract Ready.

Section 6.         Non-Competitive Procurement

A.        Emergency Contracts

In the case of an emergency, the Authority is not required to follow competitive
bidding requirements if the emergency will not permit a delay, and the
procurement of equipment, services, and supplies is necessary to respond to
the emergency. “Emergency” means a sudden, unexpected occurrence that
poses a clear and imminent danger, requiring immediate action to prevent or
mitigate the loss or impairment of life, health, property, or essential public
services. Pursuant to Public Contract Code 22050, the Board, by a four-fifths
vote, may take any immediate procurement action required by an emergency,
and may procure necessary equipment, services, and supplies without giving
notice for bids to let contracts.

In adopting this Policy, the Board authorizes the CEO to take all necessary and
proper measures in emergency conditions to repair or replace Authority
facilities as necessary. When emergency conditions do not permit a delay
resulting from a formal competitive solicitation process, the CEO is authorized
to make purchases without giving notice for bids or proposals. The CEO will
promptly report on the reasons and necessity for proceeding without a
competitive solicitation to the Board at the next available meeting after the
emergency action is taken. Board ratification is required for any contract in
excess of $500,000, and must be obtained as soon as it is practicable to do so.

B.        Lower Market Price

Pursuant to PUC § 130233, if a competitive procurement results in all bids being
rejected and the Board determines by a two-thirds vote that supplies,
equipment, and materials may be purchased at a lower price in the open
market, the Board may proceed to direct the purchase be made in the open
market.

C.        Sole Source Procurement

Regardless of the estimated cost of the procurement, the Authority is not
required to engage in the competitive procurement process, either formal or
informal, when a competitive procurement is infeasible and at least one of the
following conditions apply:

     i.   The item is only available from one source.

 ii.      If one of the conditions described below applies:

          a. Unique or Innovative Concept – The offeror demonstrates a unique or

                                          8

                                                                                   46

          innovative concept or capability not available from another source.
          “Unique or Innovative Concept” means a new, novel, or changed
          concept, approach, or method that is the product of original thinking,
          the details of which are kept confidential or are patented or
          copyrighted, and is available to the Authority only from one source
          and has not in the past been available to the Authority from another
          source.

       b. Patents or Restricted Data Rights – Patent or data rights restrictions
          preclude competition.

       c. Substantial Duplication Costs – In the case of a follow-on contract for
          the continued development or production of highly specialized
          equipment and major components thereof, when it is likely that
          award to another contractor would result in substantial duplication of
          costs that are not expected to be recovered through competition.

       d. Unacceptable Delay – In the case of a follow-on contract for the
          continued development or production of a highly specialized
          equipment and major components thereof, when it is likely that
          award to another contractor would result in unacceptable delays in
          fulfilling the Authority’s needs.

iii.   After solicitation of a number of sources, the competition is determined
       inadequate.

In all cases, the Authority must verify that the particular procurement meets the
definition of a sole source and the Authority must perform a cost or price
analysis to determine the reasonableness of the price of the sole source.

Alternatively, pursuant Public Utilities Code 130237, the Board may direct the
purchase of any supply, equipment, or material without engaging in a
competitive procurement process upon a finding by two-thirds vote of the
Board that there is only a single source of procurement and that the purchase
is for the sole purpose of duplicating or replacing supply, equipment, or
material already in use.

D.     Prototype Equipment or Modifications

Pursuant to Public Utilities Code 130236, upon a finding by two-thirds vote of all
members of the Board that a competitive process would be inadequate or not
in the Authority's best interests, the Board may direct the procurement of
prototype equipment or modifications in an amount sufficient to conduct and
evaluate operational testing without further observance of any competitive
procurement requirements.

  Budget Approval process.
• Currently, for the Original Equipment

  authority is exhausted, the project manager must
  seek additional funding approval from the Board
  for that specific contract. This delays ordering of
  the components and could impact service
  availability of the F125 Locomotives.

• Revise the Contracts and
  Procurement Policy to include
  Annuals, Section 6, Item E.
• Currently, there are Contracts

  $18,764,831.

  contract authority for the Annuals, specifically for

FROM:                      Justin Fornelli, Chief, Program Delivery


SUBJECT:                   Contract No. C3166-26 FY24 Valley Track Project -
                           Recommendation to Award - Domestic Rail Solutions (DRS
                           Contracting)


Issue

New installation and/or replacement of various track elements within the Valley Subdivision
are required to maintain a state of good repair and ensure the safety and reliability of the
existing rail system and supporting infrastructure. A new contract is required through which the
various track improvements will be implemented.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the Board authorize the Chief Executive Officer to award Contract No.
C3166-26 FY24 Valley Track Project to the lowest responsive and responsible bidder, DRS
Contracting Inc., for $4,371,907 plus 10% contract contingency of $437,190.70 for a total not-
to-exceed amount of $4,809,097.70. This recommendation is subject to the resolution of any
timely filed protest.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:


      Safety is Foundational: We will stay on the leading edge by performing improvements
      to our track system to enhance the safety of our riders, our fellow employees, and the
      communities we serve. This contract will reduce train delays and interruptions while
      increasing safety by maintaining our rail assets in a state of good repair.




                                                                                                      61

Background

The Authority proposes to rehabilitate and replace sections of track infrastructure along
various locations on the Valley Subdivision. The Valley Subdivision serves Metrolink's
Antelope Valley Line, Amtrak intercity trains, and UPRR Railway freight trains. Work under
Contract No. C3166-26 will include track rehabilitation to various elements including rail
replacement, tie replacements, and crossing rehabilitation throughout the Valley Subdivision.
These improvements will enhance the safety and reliability of Metrolink’s railway system and
maintain our rail assets in a state of good repair.


Discussion

On January 16, 2026, the Authority issued Invitation for Bids (IFB) C3166-26 for the FY24
Valley Track Project. The IFB was posted on the Authority's solicitation portal and advertised
in publications in the five-member counties. Notices were sent directly to 1,295 firms
registered in the Authority's online vendor database. Sixty firms downloaded the solicitation.
Representatives from 20 firms attended the pre-bid meeting conducted on January 28, 2026.
The Authority provided a virtual job walk video link. Four bids were received on the February
27, 2026, due date. DRS Contracting, Inc. was found to be the lowest responsive and
responsible bidder. DRS Contracting's bid amount was 10% below the Authority's
Independent Cost Estimate (ICE) and, pursuant to price analysis, was found to be fair and
reasonable. Bids were evaluated based on the total base bid plus option. The average of all
four bids was $6,214,256.84, placing our ICE within 28% of the average. Our ICE was
developed using the average bid pricing from recently awarded IFBs for similar projects. The
low bid is considered reasonable for the work to be performed.

              ICE                                              $4,847,675.00
              DRS Contracting                                  $4,371,907.00
              Balfour Beatty Infrastructure                      $4,391,192.00

              Railworks Track Systems                            $7,528,619.00
              Transdev Rail, Inc.                                $8,565,309.37



Budget Impact

The amounts for this project have been approved in the FY24 capital budget.


Next Steps

Upon approval by the Board, Staff will execute Contract No. C3166-26 for FY24 Valley Track
Project Services with DRS Contracting, Inc., in an amount not-to-exceed $4,809,097.70, and
will issue a Notice to Proceed.

ITEM ID:                   2026-153-0

TRANSMITTAL DATE:          March 20, 2026

MEETING DATE:              March 27, 2026

TO:                        Board of Directors

FROM:                      Hilary Konczal, Chief Safety, Security and Compliance Officer


SUBJECT:                   System Safety, Security, and Compliance (SSSC) Department
                           Activities - Update Q2 FY26


Issue

Staff is providing a summary of the Authority’s safety, security, and compliance activities for
Q2 for Fiscal Year (FY) 2026.

Recommendation

Receive and file.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:


      Safety is Foundational: We will stay on the leading edge by deploying new
      technologies and processes to enhance the safety and security of our riders, our fellow
      employees, and the communities we serve. Law enforcement services provide safety
      and security to the Metrolink commuter rail system and its passengers.



Background

The Authority's mission is to provide safe, efficient, dependable, and on-time transportation
service for the southern California region. The System Safety, Security, and Compliance
(SSSC) Department works to optimize the agency's safety and promote positive safety culture
in the workplace through education, engineering, and enforcement, as well as auditing and


                                                                                                     77

inspecting for safety and regulatory compliance. Using a data-informed approach, the
department utilizes leading and lagging data indicators coupled with management experience,
research, and professional expertise to understand current trends and make decisions about
the use of Agency resources in areas of focus.

Additionally, the SSSC Department tracks and evaluates inspections conducted by the
Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) and other regulatory agencies. These inspections apply
the general and permanent rules published in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR),
Transportation (Title 49 CFR Part 200-299) to oversee agency compliance and assess
penalties for violations against freight and commuter railroad agencies. The FRA conducts
inspections and audits agencies' records to monitor and enforce railroad safety regulations
specified in Title 49 CFR. The Authority places paramount importance on safety and regulation
compliance.

The primary mission of the Authority’s law enforcement services is to ensure public safety
onboard the trains, to coordinate enforcement with the cities along the Authority’s right-of-way
(ROW), and to assist with the Authority’s fare enforcement and physical security program.


Discussion


The data presented in this report reflects information submitted on the 15th of the month following the
end of quarter, in accordance with the reporting timeline specified in the law enforcement contract.


Rail Incidents
In FY26 Q2, there were fifteen (15) train strikes involving Metrolink trains, compared to nine (9)
strikes in FY26 Q1. This accounted for a 67% increase in strikes involving Metrolink trains. In
FY26 Q2, there were a total of twenty-two (22) systemwide strikes compared to a total of
seventeen (17) systemwide strikes in FY26 Q1. Overall, this is a 29% increase on systemwide
strikes.
*Systemwide strikes includes: Metrolink and foreign trains*

Incident Type                        FY26 Q1              FY26 Q2
Train vs Pedestrian                  2                    1
Train vs Trespasser                  6                    9
Train vs Vehicle                     1                    5

The SSSC Department Security staff, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department Metrolink
Bureau, and the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department also continue to focus on the
following policing strategies:
      Using current data trends, we continue to focus our Right-of-Way Enforcement activities
      at the beginning and end of the month, as well as conducting targeted enforcements at
      reported trouble areas throughout the month.
      Partnering with local police departments to increase grade-crossing enforcements and
      patrols in their area of jurisdiction, at locations where we have higher numbers of train
      strikes.



                                                                                                          78

Encouraging employees and the public to report trespassers and homeless encampments
along the right-of-way to Metrolink's Security Operations Center (SOC). These reports help us
identify locations with a higher risk of trespassing to dispatch the appropriate resources and/or
increase police patrols, relocate homeless encampments and conduct community outreach,
educating the public of the dangers of trespassing on railroad property.

Fare Evaders
FY26 Q2 fare evasion incidents are up by 10% when compared to FY26 Q1. In FY26 Q2,
there were (101) fare evasion incidents compared to ninety-two (92) incidents in FY26 Q1.

We are continuing to deploy law enforcement and contract security resources to combat fare
evasion. The security department maintains a database of incidents reported to the SOC
regarding fare evaders and unruly passengers, which include the station location and trains
where these incidents occur. Using this data, we are able to develop trends and identify where
a higher number of far evasion incidents are occurring across the system, allowing us to be
proactive and deploy security and law enforcement resources to the appropriate station, or
train. Below are a few of the successful strategies being used:
       Perform fare enforcement on board trains ensuring passengers have a valid ticket.
       Continuing "streetcaring" operations utilizing Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department
       Metrolink Bureau, San Bernardino Sheriff’s Department, and Metrolink private security.
       Platform sweeps of outlying stations, using Los Angeles County Sherriff’s Department
       Metrolink Bureau and San Bernardino Sheriff’s Department Deputies who will arrive at
       the station 10 – 15 minutes prior to the train arriving and verifying passenger fare.
       Contract security taskforce platform sweeps of outlying stations, who will arrive at the
       station 10 – 15 minutes prior to the train arriving and verifying passenger fare.
       Utilizing our contract security at Union Station and stations throughout the Metrolink
       system.

Unruly Passengers
FY26 Q2 unruly passenger incidents are down 2% compared to FY26 Q1. In FY26 Q2 there
were a total of one hundred eighty-one (181) incidents involving unruly passengers compared
to one hundred eighty-five (185) incidents in FY26 Q1.

Law Enforcement & Security Presence on Station Platforms, Trains, at Grade-
Crossings, and Right-of-Way by County and Line
A Problem Orientated Policing Strategy collects and analyzes crime data for trends and
threats, as well as other possible security related risks so we can deploy the appropriate
resources to mitigate and prevent trespassing and other crimes on the Metrolink system. We
also track the initiative-taking activities our law enforcement and contract security are
performing to ensure a safe and secure system.

matters.text:
ACTION: Upon a single motion by Vice-Chair Berkson and seconded by Director Preciado,
    the Board (11-0) approved the proposed amendment to the FY26 budget, increasing the
    Operating Budget by $914,029, and increasing the Capital Budget by $500,000.

    If approved, these amendments will result in an Amended FY26 Operating Budget. FY26
    Operating Revenue will remain at $76,914,792. Expenses will increase by $914,029,
    bringing the total to $353,337,315. Support will also increase by $914,029, bringing the
    revised total from $275,508,494 to $276,422,523. The FY26 State of Good Repair Capital
    budget will increase by $500,000, bringing the total from $137,502,000 to $138,002,000.

7.C Contract No. EP199-19 - Rebuild of Bombardier Rail Cars - Increase Contract
    Authority - Talgo-SYSTRA Joint Venture

    Project Engineer I Christian Velez requested additional contract authority to complete the
    rebuild of the 33 remaining Bombardier rail cars (26 Generation-3 and 7 Generation-2) in
    order to maintain program continuity, avoid delays, and complete the rebuild in the most
    efficient and cost-effective manner to keep the Bombardier fleet in a State of Good Repair.

    Director Marquez asked if all the cars will be at a certain level by the Olympics in 2028.

    Mr. Velez confirmed the 88 Generation-1 cars and 24 of the 26 Generation-3 cars are
    expected to be completed before the Olympics.

    Director Marquez asked if the exterior of some of the cars will be refurbished.

    Mr. Velez stated they will be repainted with the new Metrolink scheme under this scope of
    work.

    Mr. Kettle noted some equipment’s rehabilitation may be postponed leading up to the
    Olympics in order to be available for service.

    Second Vice-Chair Trembley noted the multiple scenarios considered in the staff report and
    asked if “procurement risk” was quantified as it was a factor in the recommendation.

    Mr. Velez stated it was based off of historic estimates that would lead to a year in procurement
    if another contractor could even be identified to do the work.

    Second Vice-Chair Trembley stated the staff recommendation is based off exercising this
    particular option as being the lowest risk and avoiding delay and asked what was the greatest
    criteria staff used in making the recommendation. He wondered if it was timely delivery prior
    to the 2028 Olympics.

    Senior Contract and Compliance Administrator Dorothea Cantero explained one factor was
    making sure every piece of equipment is available for the Olympics, but “procurement risk”
    means Metrolink would lose another year before the equipment could be overhauled.

    Second Vice-Chair Trembley asked if the primary driver for the recommendation is having
    these deliverables for the Olympics. He balanced that against what staff thought would be the
    lesser overall cost in going with an overhaul contract. He opined this is an example of the
    agency is spending more money as opposed to the alternative just to ensure these cars are
    available on a timely basis for the Olympics.

                                                                                                       141
                                                4

    Chief of Program Delivery Justin Fornelli explained Olympics readiness is one of many factors
    staff took into account. One of the big things considered was the build quality of these cars
    with the existing contractor has been phenomenal and having the same vendor provide the
    same overhaul and improvement ensures the same systems and parts throughout the entire
    fleet. He emphasized the systems, parts, and overall build quality was a larger consideration.

    Second Vice-Chair Trembley wanted to know the criteria because this would be another
    example of spending more money with the 2028 Olympics as the driver and he was concerned
    with the lack of support from the federal government to-date.

    Mr. Fornelli confirmed the continuity and quality of work is the primary weight in this decision.

    Director Dutrey complimented the Bombardier refurbishment as he rode one that morning and
    it looks brand new. He asked about the timeframe to refurbish or replace the newer Rotem
    cars.

    Mr. Velez explained those cars are just reaching midlife and there is money set aside for them,
    but staff is waiting to get those cars overhauled.

    ACTION: Upon a single motion by Director Dutrey and seconded by Director Preciado, the
    Board (11-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to amend Contract No. EP199-19 with
    Talgo-SYSTRA Joint Venture to exercise Option Order No. 2, supporting the rebuild of 26
    Generation-3 Bombardier rail cars, and provide contract provisions to award future options
    as funding becomes available to complete the remaining 7 Generation-2 Bombardier rail
    cars.

    This action requires the contract authority to be increased by a total of $83,360,742.82,
    inclusive of 10% contingency, increasing the total contract authority amount from
    $152,871,246.50 to $236,231,989.32, which will allow for the remaining 33 Bombardier Rail
    Cars (26 Generation-3 cars as Option Order No. 2 and 7 Generation-2 cars as a future
    option orders when funding becomes available) to be rebuilt. The requested contract
    authority is included in the Adopted Capital Budget for FY20-21 & FY23–26 for Option Order
    2, contingent upon a Project Budget Reallocation (PBR) from other equipment projects that
    have been deferred. The Future Option Orders will be included in future Capital Budgets,
    subject to Board approval.

7.D Contract No. EP249-26 - Cab Room Camera and Locomotive Digital Video Recorder
    System Replacement - Recommendation to Award - Railhead Corporation

    Kevin Bleich, Project Engineer I, explained the cab camera and locomotive digital video
    recorder (LDVR) system currently installed in Metrolink's fleet is obsolete and in need of
    replacement. In addition, a new Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) regulation going into
    effect in October 2027 requires the addition of crash hardened memory to the LDVR system.
    This project will ensure the Authority is in compliance with the new regulation in addition to
    upgrading the aging system.

    Director McCallon asked why the contingency is 20%.

    Mr. Bleich stated the FRA deadline is coming up soon and staff wants to ensure the agency
    is covered should anything come up during installations as the deadline approaches.


                                                                                                        142
                                                5

    Mr. Fornelli furthered the contingency provides flexibility in case any issues arise, the money
    can be used to advance the program. The concern with the deadline is any cars that don’t
    have the system in place have to be parked. This allows Program Delivery to support
    Operations to make sure all equipment is available.

    Mr. Kettle added because of the short timeframe, the contractor may dip into the contingency
    quicker because they’re doing more work faster.

    Director Spiegel received confirmation that the contingency covers the need for additional
    needed money without getting board approval.

    ACTION: Upon a single motion by Director McCallon and seconded by Second Vice-Chair
    Trembley, the Board (11-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and execute
    Contract No. EP249-26 for Cab Room Camera and Locomotive Digital Video Recorder
    System Replacement with Railhead Corporation in the amount of $1,727,696 plus a 20%
    contingency of $345,539.20, for a total not-to-exceed contract authority of $2,073,235.20.
    This award is subject to resolution of any timely filed protests.

    The not-to-exceed amount of $1,727,696 (including Options) plus 20% contingency for a
    total of $2,073,235.20 is included in the Capital Budgets for FY19, FY24, and FY25, which
    were adopted by the Board.

7.E Fiscal Year 2024-25 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and Single Audit

    The Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) and Single Audit for Fiscal Year 2024-
    25 have been completed.

    Director McCallon asked about the finding regarding management override of internal
    controls from a fraud standpoint as it is a significant risk that was identified.

    Eide Bailly Senior Manager Kyle Bartle clarified in professional audit standards identifying
    risk is part of specific audit procedures. Some meet the criteria of “significant risk” which
    used to be documented internally, but the auditing standards changed and now they have
    to be disclosed if they are considered to be “significant risks.” The three items, beginning
    with management override of internal controls, is a risk that is inherent to all organizations
    that rely upon internal controls for preparation and reporting of financial transactions. He
    confirmed it is nothing unique to Metrolink, it is inherent to every single organization that is
    audited. He added if there was an issue with management’s controls, they would be reported
    as a finding and would include a recommendation.

    Director Dutrey asked about the risks associated with estimated pension amounts.

    Mr. Bartle explained in the preparation of the financial statements there are certain estimates
    that management must rely upon and they rise to a level of “significant estimate” based upon
    subjective criteria. It’s not because of the nature of Metrolink’s unique estimates being used,
    it’s inherent because those relate to pensions and other post-employment benefits which
    rely upon an actuary and assumptions to project a long-term amount that fluctuates
    significantly every year.

    The Board received and filed this report.


                                                                                                       143
                                                6

7.F FY26 Monthly Report of Ridership, Revenue, and Financial Results for December 2025

    Ms. Wilson shared the ridership performance and financial results through December. She
    went over ridership and farebox revenue recovery, operating statement results, budget
    savings and cost avoidance, and Arrow Service’s revenue and operating statement. She
    shared results of the refreshed Sperry Capital/KPMG forecast of ridership and revenue. She
    touched on the accounts receivables past due and the agency’s cash position and provided
    a ridership update.

    The Board received and filed this report.

7.G Metrolink 2025 Onboard Survey - Summary of Key Findings

    Henning Eichler, Senior Manager, Market Insights and Analytics, shared the results of a
    systemwide onboard customer survey that was conducted in June 2025 to update ridership
    demographics and travel patterns. He highlighted the key insights about Metrolink’s post-
    pandemic ridership base, and significant changes since the pandemic. He shared the
    change in demographics, non-commuter trips, and the vision of sustainable growth to serve
    riders’ needs.

    Director Dutrey noted more riders are dependent on the system, are also dependent on
    subsidies and the low-income fare has become a need for riders.

    Mr. Eichler confirmed those riders have responded to the discounts staff has recommended
    and the hope for student riders is they will continue to ride when they gain employment.

    Director Dutrey opined one of the challenges the Board faces is fare revenue is dropping
    and that requires member agencies to increase subsidies. He asked what happens if an
    agency can't afford their subsidies and needs to reduce support and if there will be service
    reductions.

    Mr. Kettle stated everything is on the table and there are challenges on the revenue side as
    it relates to ridership. Metrolink has notices from two member agencies – one official and
    one unofficial – so it is going to be a really challenging budget year for Metrolink as an
    agency. Staff is looking at a variety of options, one of which may be service reduction, and
    another might be fare increases, which the agency has not done in 12 years.

    Director Spiegel added Riverside is looking for additional service and is still strong
    supporters of Metrolink. She emphasized regardless of age, regardless of going to work,
    time is a factor that the agency needs to focus on. She urged looking into the reason for
    constant delays to get people back on trains that are reliable.

    Mr. Kettle agreed the fundamentals of safety, cleanliness, and reliability are at the core of
    what riders need. He conceded Metrolink struggled with on-time performance the second
    half of 2025, but is at about 95% responsible on-time performance for the month of February.
    Staff is working with the mechanical and operations teams and is seeing some progress
    because reliability is something that matters to customers.




                                                                                                    144
                                                7

    Director Marquez noticed he has had to pay for parking this past year going out of Pomona
    and asked if this is happening at all stations or just North Pomona.

    Mr. Kettle stated at this point just North Pomona charges for parking, which was something
    put in place by LA Metro with the extension of the A Line because of what was anticipated
    to be an increased need for parking.

    Director Marquez complained the parking is no longer for Metrolink so riders no longer have
    the spaces they used to have.

    Mr. Kettle confirmed Metrolink parking is no longer free because the parking lot cannot be
    divided by paid and free. He stated the stations are owned by the local community and LA
    Metro instigated paid parking in this instance.

    Director Marquez asked if Metrolink sees any of the monies that are paid for parking.

    Mr. Kettle stated Metrolink does not get a share of the fees and recommended Director
    Marquez park at Montclair.

    Director Najarian opined that “instigated” is a tough word being thrown at LA Metro and
    suggested asking Director Sandoval, who is the Mayor of Pomona, about it at the next meeting.

    The Board received and filed this report.

7.H February Legislative Update

    Government and Community Relations Director Jeff Dunn provided a regular monthly
    update on current legislative affairs. He touched on SB 667 which would require railroads to
    install and operate wayside detector systems every ten miles on or adjacent to track used
    by freight train and non-compliance would result in a 10 MPH speed limit. The bill passed
    the senate in January and is now in the assembly not yet referred to committee. He went
    over the introduction of other bills that impact transit. On February 18 the Subcommittee on
    LOSSAN Rail Corridor Resiliency held an informational hearing strengthening governance
    and performance of southern California rail and CEO Kettle provided testimony.

    Mr. Kettle provided an overview of his experience at the Subcommittee. He stated Chair
    Blakespear asked a number of questions about the challenges Metrolink is facing that were
    discussed during Mr. Eichler’s presentation. He shared the fiscal challenges and why the
    agency has not asked Sacramento for additional resources. He explained a little bit about
    the governance structure and fiscal process as a five-county system and JPA and the
    significant need for additional resources to continue rail operations even at a status quo
    level.

    Mr. Dunn stated staff received deep appreciation from the senators and staff for Mr. Kettle’s
    time and expertise to assist the Committee’s role in dealing with the challenges that are
    endemic to the region.

    Director McCallon moved that Metrolink takes a position of opposing SB 667.




                                                                                                    145
                                                8

Chair Chaffee asked if the bill be amended or if it is a bad bill.

Mr. Dunn explained it is considered judgment that the bill cannot be amended to make it
acceptable to CTA or to Metrolink.

Director Preciado asked if it is being opposed because there’s no funding for it.

Mr. Dunn agreed it would impose an unfunded mandate of $5M just to implement the
program on the system along with ongoing implementation costs. The prescriptive nature of
the bill (slowing trains down to 10 MPH) is completely unworkable both on the passenger
and the freight side. He explained this bill was introduced principally to address freight
railroads in the wake of the Palestine (Ohio) incident, but it has very real impacts on
Metrolink as a passenger rail agency. There have been zero instances of loss of life or
property on passenger railroad in the United States in history due to the failure of these
particular pieces of equipment the bill is trying to bolster up. He concluded all these factors
are causing considerable consternation in the passenger rail space.

Director Trembley asked what a wayside detector is.

Chief Operating Officer Don Filippi clarified there are multiple types. The high wide will detect
if a load is too high or too wide for a section of track and will alert to stop the train so there
isn’t any damage. A hot box detector will determine if a wheel, axel, or journal is overheating
which could result in a derailment. He explained the hot box is the one in reference to the bill.

ACTION: Upon a single motion by Director McCallon and seconded by Second Vice-Chair
Trembley, the Board (11-0) took the position of OPPOSE SB 667 related to the wayside
detector mandate.

Director Spiegel asked if incentivized transit-oriented developments are part of the bill
mentioned by Mr. Dunn.

Mr. Dunn explained that there is different legislation and there are a couple of intent bills
intended to clean up legislation from last year and staff is monitoring them.

Director Spiegel asked if it has been proven there is an increase in ridership by creating transit-
oriented development and she wondered who receives the incentive.

Mr. Dunn stated developers and municipalities receive the incentives dependent upon the
legislation. He added there was consternation and lack of clarity in the bill that passed last
year by Senator Wiener so that is underlying the cleanup efforts this year.

Director Spiegel opined when Sacramento is trying to dictate and take over local control the
local jurisdictions are just told what to do with no support for mandates. She requested staff
keep their ears open because she cannot support any bills that take away local control.

Director Allen agreed and noted the League of California Cities opposed SB 79 as it is a local
control issue. Covina did surveys of housing multiple units next to the station and the results
did not align with Senator Wiener’s assessment and he opined it was a bad bill and most cities
opposed it.



                                                                                                      146
                                             9

SUBJECT:                  Contract No. EP249-26 - Cab Room Camera and Locomotive
                          Digital   Video   Recorder    System    Replacement  -
                          Recommendation to Award - Railhead Corporation


Issue

The cab camera and Locomotive Digital Video Recorder (LDVR) system currently installed in
Metrolink's fleet is obsolete and in need of replacement. In addition, a new Federal Railroad
Administration (FRA) regulation going into effect in October 2027 requires the addition of
crash hardened memory to the LDVR system. This project will ensure the Authority is in
compliance with the new regulation in addition to upgrading the aging system on our fleet.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the Board authorize the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and
execute Contract No. EP249-26 for Cab Room Camera and Locomotive Digital Video
Recorder System Replacement with Railhead Corporation in the amount of $1,727,696 plus a
20% contingency of $345,539.20, for a total not-to-exceed contract authority of $2,073,235.20.
This award is subject to resolution of any timely filed protests.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan Commitment of:

      Safety is Foundational: We will stay on the leading edge by deploying new
      technologies and processes to enhance the safety and security of our riders, our fellow
      employees, and the communities we serve. This project will upgrade the cab camera
      and LDVR system on the Authority's fleet to ensure compliance with FRA regulations.




                                                                                                    62

Background

Currently, the Authority has an LDVR system including two inward-facing cameras and one
forward-facing camera in each locomotive and cab car to ensure operator compliance and for
accident investigations. The components of the existing system have become obsolete, with
increasing failure rates in recent years. Additionally, a new FRA regulation which takes effect
on October 12, 2027, requires passenger train locomotives and cab cars to be equipped with
inward and outward facing cameras and an LDVR system with crash hardened memory. This
project addresses both items by providing a new FRA-compliant LDVR system to replace the
existing components on the Authority's fleet of locomotives and cab cars.


Discussion

Capital Equipment staff submitted their request for new procurement on August 11, 2025. It
was determined that a Request for Proposal (RFP) method should be used in order to allow
for different equipment and approaches to meet the Authority’s needs and the FRA standards.
The RFP was issued on September 17, 2025. One site visit was held on September 30 to
allow the prospective proposers to look over all of the different models of equipment. A total of
67 questions were received by the deadline. All of the questions were answered by staff and
issued on November 4.

On November 25, six proposals were received, all were found to be responsive and
responsible. These proposals were sent to the evaluation committee for technical review. Four
of the six proposals were found to be technically acceptable. Presentations by the four
technically acceptable proposers were conducted on the week of January 19, 2026, and
technical and price scoring was completed on January 23, 2026. A summary of the scoring is
in the table below:

Price Score                 14.33            20.00             4.66               10.91
Total Score                 76.53            83.40             65.06              75.91
Rank                          2                 1                4                  3

Following the selection of the highest ranked proposer, staff began negotiations with Railhead
Corporation. Pricing, testing and composition of the kits were discussed as well as the
possible options for additional units and installation services. The pricing breakdown is listed
on the table below:
                Phase & Equipment                             ICE          Railhead Corporation
Base Order: Hyundai-Rotem Cab Car                          $1,808,840.00            $663,252.00
Base Order: F125 Locomotive                                $1,295,440.00            $465,440.00
Base Order: MP36PH-3C Locomotive                             $540,440.00            $174,540.00
Base Order: F59PHR Locomotive                                $238,440.00             $58,180.00
                                  Base Order Total         $3,883,160.00          $1,361,412.00
Option Order 1: Spares                                       $450,000.00            $174,540.00


                                                                                                    63

Option Order 2: Installation of all units                 $790,005.00           $145,200.00
Option Order 3: Stadler DMU & ZEMU                        $329,040.00            $46,544.00
                                Option Orders Total     $1,569,045.00           $366,284.00
                   Grand Total                          $5,452,205.00         $1,727,696.00
                   Over / Under                                              -68.31%

The proposed price from Railhead was 68.31% below the Independent Cost Estimate (ICE).
As such Staff met with Railhead to go over the individual cost items. Railhead confirmed that
several individual cost items listed in the ICE such as warranty, engineering, training and
documentation were built into the price of each individual kit. As the current and previous
contractor for the Authority's fleet they already have the necessary technical drawings and
measurements on the Authority's equipment. Railhead confirmed that all deliverables and
requirements would be met. After this discussion the price was found to be fair and
reasonable.


Budget Impact

The not-to-exceed amount of $1,727,696 (including Options) plus 20% contingency for a total
of $2,073,235.20 is included in the Capital Budgets for FY19, FY24, and FY25, which were
adopted by the Board.


Next Steps

Upon Board approval of the recommendation, staff will execute a contract with Railhead
Corporation and issue Notice to Proceed. The base period of the project is expected to be
completed within 270 days from NTP.

     were absent.

7A. Contract No. SP614-25 - IT Staff Augmentation Services - Recommendation to Award

     to augment critical staff in providing agency technology services, including the delivery of
     internal computing systems, technologies, and enterprise applications.

     ACTION: Upon a single motion by Director Sandoval and seconded by Director Dutrey, the

7B. Purchase Order MTL2606717 - Sole Source procurement of a C175-20 Locomotive
    Engine - Progress Rail Locomotive Inc.

     Chief Financial Officer Tom Schamber provided background on an additional C175-20
     engine needed to increase Materials Management’s spare core pool for the F125
     locomotives.

     Director Spiegel noted the 54-week lead time.

     Mr. Schamber explained it’s hard to balance and maintain the inventory of these parts as
     they’re all one-offs and unique to the F-125 and Progress Rail doesn’t keep them on hand.

     Director Spiegel asked how many engines will be overhauled.

     Chief Operating Officer Don Filippi explained there are 40 F-125 and the OEM requires they
     be overhauled every 18,000 miles or every four years and spares are needed to keep
     service running.

     Board (10-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and award Sole Source

11B. Purchase Order No. PO1027- 26 - Signal Maintainer and Mechanic Trucks -

     The Authority requires these vehicles for the Maintenance of Way and Equipment
     departments to effectively support railroad operations. Several vehicles in the Authority's
     fleet used by these departments have exceeded their useful life and are experiencing
     increasing reliability issues, creating operational inefficiencies and elevated safety risks. In

     support the current scope of work for these departments.

    electrical switchgear at the Central Maintenance Facility (CMF), located at 1555 N. San
    Fernando Road, Los Angeles, CA 90065. Both systems contain components that have
    reached the end of their service life, frequently require repairs, or have otherwise become
    obsolete, and must therefore be replaced to ensure safety, reliability, and compliance with
    current standards.

    The Board (10-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to award Contract No. C3157R-
    26 Fire Alarm and Switchgear Replacement Project to the lowest responsive and
    responsible bidder, Golden Phoenix Construction in the amount of $1,687,050, consisting
    of the bid amount of $1,467,000 plus a 15% contingency of $220,050.

    The amounts for which contract authority is requested are included in the adopted Capital
    Budget for FY20, FY23, and FY24.

11D. Contract Nos. PO1011A-26, PO1011B-26, PO1011C-26, and PO1011D- 26 - Oils,
     Coolants, and Lubricants - Recommendation to Award - AAA Oil, Inc, Blue Angel
     International LLC, Hasco Oil Company, and XTT Life, LLC.

    The Authority requires a range of oils, coolants, and lubricants to operate and maintain its
    fleet of locomotives.

    The Board (10-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to award the following contracts
    with their respective not-to-exceed contract authority (total for the base and option periods):
    1. Contract No. PO1011A-26: AAA Oil, Inc - $130,000
    2. Contract No. PO1011B-26: Blue Angel International LLC - $10,000
    3. Contract No. PO1011C-26: Hasco Oil Company - $1,300,000
    4. Contract No. PO1011D-26: XTT Life, LLC - $44,000

    These contracts will have a base term of one- year, with a single one-year option that will
    be exercised at the sole discretion of the Chief Executive Officer if deemed to be in the
    Authority's best interest. This award is subject to resolution of any timely received protests.

    The cost of the oils, coolants, and lubricants that will be purchased under these contracts
    will be covered by the Materials Management operating budget for Fiscal Years 2026 and
    2027 for the base term, and Fiscal Years 2027 and 2028 for the option term if exercised.
    Expenditure of amounts for FY27 and FY28 are contingent upon budget adoption covering
    that period.

11E. Grants Quarterly Update - 2nd Quarter, FY 2026

    Staff is providing an update of grant acquisition, reprogramming and closeout activity for
    the period of October 1, 2025 to December 31, 2025.

                                                                                                      425
                                                5

    compensation matters.

     Officer's Authority

    Policies (Revised Policies) on November 8, 2019. Section 3 of the Revised Policies

    of $500,000.

                                                                                                 426
                                                6

     Staff is providing an update on the progress of the Authority’s Capital Program, including
     the Southern California Optimized Rail Expansion (SCORE) Program and the State of
     Good Repair Program.

     The Board received and filed this report.

12. WORKSHOP PRESENTATIONS

     Chair Chaffee welcomed the Board to the workshop and introduced the board and executive
     team to the book How to Hug a Porcupine and urged everyone to be kind to themselves and
     others and have an open dialogue to make Metrolink better.

     Mr. Kettle added the day’s workshop will focus on real-time issues impacting Metrolink.

A. State and Federal Advocates Overview on Legislative and Executive Initiatives in
   Sacramento and Washington, D.C.

     Advocates provided an overview of matters going on at the Federal and State levels. Rick
     Alcalde of Potomac Partners DC discussed the Highway Bill and federal funding and the
     IIJA. Chris Kierig of Kadesh & Associates spoke about the past year of appropriations and
     Metrolink’s engagement in Washington, D.C. Donald Norden and Genevieve Cowan from
     Blank Rome touched on national railroad issues and regulatory proceedings and
     transportation bipartisanship. They provided examples of their firm assisting Metrolink.

     Andrew Antwih, Shaw Yoder Antwih Schmelzer & Lange spoke about the Governor’s State
     of the State speech and changes in senate legislature. Mark Watts, Watts & Hartmann, LLC,
     discussed Local Transportation Fund (LTF) allocations and the Transit Transformation
     Taskforce along with Senate Bill 79 related to housing developments located near specified
     transit stops.

     The Board recessed at 11:05 a.m. and reconvened at 11:14 a.m.

B.   Operations Briefing

     Chief Operating Officer Don Filippi provided an overview of his department’s challenges and
     service issues. He went over terminology, performance metrics systemwide and by line, top
     reasons for annulled and terminated trains, and challenges on foreign railroads. He went
     into detail about vandalism and its impacts and maintenance and equipment challenges with
     an aging fleet, materials shortages, depleted inventory, and cannibalization of parts. He
     explained the complexity of having three types of locomotives, and the overhaul
     requirements of the F-125. He noted Alstom is working behind the scenes to work around
     the parts failures to support Metrolink. He underlined the materials shortages and limited
     inventory and how the cannibalization of fleet lowers reliability.

     Board discussion included communications with the freight railroads and looking into freight
     consolidators; advocating for stiffer penalties for copper wire theft; having Alstom leverage
     their position as a global parts supplier to ease the burden. There was further discussion
     about the F-125 and its overhaul schedule along with the future of buying other Tier 4
     locomotives and the potential to move away from the F-125.
                                                                                                     427
                                                 7

   Director Sandoval commended Mr. Filippi for his passion, care, and advocation and desire
   to make Metrolink a better system.

   Director Wapner stated he does not like a “pay as you go system” and asked why the capital
   replacement is not included in the budget process.

   Mr. Kettle explained it took quite some time to get the capital reserve so that we have a
   working capital fund, and he hoped conversations like this will urge board members to go
   back to their member agencies and remind them what it takes to run a sustainable regional
   passenger rail system by advocating for Metrolink.

   Justin Fornelli, Chief of Program Delivery, explained the State of Good Repair program staff
   has identified a capital projects backlog of $900M and $150M annually to maintain status quo.

   The Board recessed at 12:32 p.m. and reconvened at 12:41 p.m.

C. Financial Update and FY27 Budget Development

   Chief Financial Officer Tom Schamber explained farebox revenues are not recovering
   quickly and operating expenses and member agency support are rising, and recent on-
   time performance issues are factors in service delivery and ridership. He furthered member
   agency local sales tax receipts are not meeting forecasts and state transit funding is not
   keeping pace with the economic realities of the industry. He provided an overview of where
   funding comes from and highest agency costs. He touched on farebox recovery compared
   with other agencies and operating cost per passenger mile, noting Metrolink has not raised
   fares in several years. He went over the budget assumptions and timeline for creating the
   FY27 budget.

   Mr. Kettle clarified Scenario 2 of the budget assumptions is in reference to a letter from
   OCTA’s CEO putting Metrolink on notice that OCTA’s member agency support would be
   reduced by 10% for FY27. He recognized there may be service reductions to meet the
   reduced member agency support from OCTA. He relayed a conversation with RCTC’s
   executive director to maintain the service level assumptions that expand service and grow
   ridership in Riverside County and the desire to be held harmless in the development of
   Scenario 2. Metrolink will be working with OCTA staff to work towards something that
   recognizes the interest of all member agencies over the next two to three months.

   Mr. Schamber confirmed for Director Spiegel that reducing the cannibalization of parts will
   improve the reliability and reduce costs for the agency.

   Director Spiegel asked if OCTA reducing their support by 10% is actually 15% including the
   5% annual increase all the member agencies pay.

   Mr. Kettle explained it is complicated as the agency still has to develop analysis with OCTA
   staff so there is full understanding what this means for them and other agencies by
   transferring fixed costs to other agencies based on the all-share formulas.

   Director Lyndes asked if there will be federal funding trickling down for the World Cup.

   Mr. Kettle explained based on the formulas, the LA area would receive about $9M and it
   has not been figured out how it will be distributed.
                                                                                                   428
                                              8

D. World Cup and 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games Update

   Special Projects Director Michael Litschi provided an overview of the 2026 FIFA World
   Cup, including locations, anticipated spectators, match schedules at SoFi Stadium, and
   proposed Fan Fests and Zones. He presented the needed security funding request and
   forthcoming threat and vulnerability assessment. He set the stage for the 2028 Olympic
   Games, times, venues, service scenarios, and the request for federal funding for expanded
   service during the Games. He noted staff is developing an MOU between LA28 and
   Metrolink outlining each agency’s respective roles and responsibilities for Games delivery.

E. Service Growth Development Plan (SGDP) Update – Pushed to February

13. ADJOURNMENT

   There being no further business for consideration by the Board, the meeting was adjourned
   at 1:32 p.m.

   Prepared by,


   Michelle Peña
   Board Clerk

SUBJECT:                   Contract No. SP614-25 - IT Staff Augmentation Services -
                           Recommendation to Award Bench Contract


Issue

The Authority requires a bench of consultants to augment current staff in providing agency
technology services, including the delivery of internal computing systems, technologies, and
enterprise applications.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the Board authorize the Chief Executive Officer to:
    1. Award Bench Contract No. SP614-25 for IT Staff Augmentation Services as follows:
        SP614A-25 Computer Aid, Inc.,
        SP614B-25 ICF Incorporated, LLC,
        SP614C-25 Infojini Consulting, Inc.,
        SP614D-25 Intratek Computer, Inc.,
        SP614E-25 Tryfacta, Inc. and;
    2. Approve a total not-to-exceed Bench Contract authority amount of $7,386,120 for a base
        of three years with two one-year options that may be exercised by the CEO at the sole
        discretion of the Authority. Work under this contract will be authorized through the CTO
        process on an as needed basis.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Modernizing Business Practices: We will improve our operational efficiency through



                                                                                                      8

     transparency, objective metrics and streamlined governance, reducing over-reliance on
     subsidy while bringing our system into a state of good repair and investing in the
     development of our employees.


Background

Since 2016 Metrolink has used bench contracts to augment staffing for the Integrated Digital
and Technology Services department (IDTS). Contracted positions included Helpdesk
Technicians, Database Administrators, Network Engineers, System Administrators and
Application Developers.

The current contract ends May 31st, 2026. The new bench introduces modern roles and
updated role descriptions to align with contemporary technology service delivery frameworks.
The new contract also provides a new group of service providers who are identified as well-
positioned to deliver improved services that support Metrolink's focus on and dedication to
superior technology service delivery and innovation.


Discussion

On February 10, 2025, the Authority released a Request for Proposal (RFP) for IT Staff
Augmentation services on an on-call basis for a contract term of three years with two one-year
options. The solicitation was published in the five member counties, as well as posted on the
Authority’s online procurement module. Notices were also emailed to firms registered on the
Authority’s online procurement module. 344 vendors were notified and 328 downloaded the
solicitation. On February 26, 2025 a pre-proposal conference was held with 70 attendants
representing 58 firms. The Authority received and answered 364 questions. A record number
of 144 proposals were received by the due date of May 8, 2025.

Proposals were independently reviewed by two Senior Contract & Compliance Administrators
to determine responsiveness. Seventeen (17) firms were found responsive and moved on to
the evaluation phase.

Proposals were evaluated in accordance with the Authority's procurement policies and
procedures. A Technical Evaluation Committee, consisting of five Authority staff members,
reviewed and scored the technical proposals and 13 firms met the minimum qualifications with
a technical score of 56 or greater, per the RFP requirements. Per the RFP, the top ten scored
proposers proceeded to the interview phase. Technical scores were subject to an adjustment
based on information learned from the interview. Price scores were calculated based on the
advertised calculation formula to form the final scores of the top 10 as follows:

SUBJECT:                  Purchase Order MTL2606717 - Sole Source procurement of a
                          C175-20 Locomotive Engine - Progress Rail Locomotive Inc.


Issue

The Authority's Materials Management Department needs an additional C175-20 engine to
increase its spare core pool for the F125 locomotives.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the Board authorize the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and award
Sole Source Purchase Order MTL2606717 to Progress Rail Locomotive Inc. in a total not-to-
exceed amount of $1,100,000 for the purchase of a new C175-20 Locomotive Engine.


Strategic Commitment

The report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Customer Are Our Business: We respect and value our customers, putting them at the
      heart of all we do, and work hard to attract and retain new customers by understanding
      their needs and find new and innovative ways to delight them. The purchase of a spare
      engine will ensure that the materials management department has enough engines
      available to support timely maintenance of the F125 Locomotive fleet.


Background

The F125 Locomotive fleet is undergoing a manufacturer recommended 18,000 service-hour
overhaul. Currently the Authority owns three spare engines cores. Due to the overhaul



                                                                                                   15

project's schedule and capacity, as well as the fact that several in-service engines are already
operating beyond the recommended overhaul point, it is absolutely necessary to add another
C175-20 engine to the available core pool to support the overhaul project, as well as any
potential engine failure.

The Finance department's Materials Management unit is responsible for the procurement of
parts and other resources needed to operate the Authority's fleet. Staff is working closely with
the Operations department to develop a strategic approach to materials procurement to
ensure we have what we need, when we need it, to run reliable and safe service. This engine
purchase is an outcome of that effort, and such decision-making will continue to be applied
during the FY27 budget process and beyond.


Discussion

Although Caterpillar is the manufacturer of the C175-20 engines powering the F125
locomotives, Progress Rail Locomotive Inc. is the manufacturer of the locomotive and the only
Caterpillar authorized dealer to sell new C175-20 engines to the Authority. The supplier has a
54-week lead time for this engine. Should this request be approved, delivery will likely happen
in 2027.


Budget Impact

The amount for which contract authority is requested was included in the proposed Materials
Management FY27 operating budget.


Next Steps

Upon approval by the Board, Staff will reach out to Progress Rail Locomotive Inc. to negotiate
pricing and issue a purchase order for the engine.

FROM:                       Paul Hubler, Chief Strategy Officer


SUBJECT:                    January Legislative Update


Issue

Staff provides a regular monthly update on current legislative affairs.

Recommendation

Receive and file.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitments of:

      Connecting and Leveraging Partnerships: We will forge new and enhanced
      relationships with our public and private partners to integrate and coordinate connecting
      services, providing residents throughout Southern California with better, seamless,
      sustainable alternatives to driving. This commitment is met by sharing news, information
      and the Authority’s legislative priorities with elected officials.

      Advancing Key Regional Goals: We will grow the role of regional rail in addressing
      climate change, air quality, and other pressing issues by advancing toward zero
      emissions, making rail a compelling alternative to single-occupant automobiles and
      advancing equity-focused opportunities for all communities throughout Southern
      California. This commitment is met by encouraging federal, state and local support for
      Authority priorities.


Background



                                                                                                        22

Staff continues to engage with community, local, state, and federal stakeholders concerning
Metrolink service and relevant policy initiatives.


Discussion

State

Transit Transportation Task Force Releases Final Report
Senate Bill 125, the Fiscal Year 2023–24 budget bill, required the California State
Transportation Agency (CalSTA) to establish and convene the Transit Transformation Task
Force (TTTF) to develop a structured, coordinated process for engaging transit agencies and
stakeholders and to advance policy recommendations to grow ridership and strengthen public
transit statewide. The 25-member task force, composed of representatives from CalSTA, local
agencies, academic institutions, nongovernmental organizations, and other transportation
stakeholders, met 13 times between December 2023 and September 2025, to examine key
policy and funding challenges, including statutorily required analysis of potential reforms to the
Transportation Development Act (TDA).

On October 29, 2025, Metrolink submitted a letter to CalSTA Secretary Toks Omishakin
responding to the draft report and emphasizing the need for dedicated, sustainable revenue
solutions to ensure the long-term viability of California’s transit systems. The final TTTF report,
released in December 2025, outlines a vision for transforming public transit into a reliable,
accessible, and dignified alternative to driving and provides strategic direction. However, the
report does not recommend finalized funding or TDA policy proposals but rather a starting
point for future conversation.

Second Year of Legislative Session Begins
The legislature reconvened on January 5, 2026 for the second year of the 2025-26 session.
Some bills that were introduced in 2025, but did not move forward beyond certain deadlines,
may be brought up for a vote this month. In 2026, bills must be approved no later than August
31, and the Governor must sign or veto bills by the end of September.

Each year, the state’s Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) publishes a fiscal outlook in
anticipation of the upcoming budget season. The report is an independent assessment of
revenues and spending with the goal of preparing lawmakers with an analysis of the state’s
General Fund budget condition. The LAO is projecting the state will face a $18 billion budget
deficit due to higher spending and federal cuts, even though the state has seen overall
revenue growth. Governor Newsom will release the proposed budget for the upcoming fiscal
year 2026-27 by January 10, 2026.

Federal

FY26 Funding Update
When Congress voted to reopen the federal government in November, it passed a Continuing
Resolution (CR) to fund operations through January 30, allowing time to negotiate FY26
funding levels. In the weeks that followed, Senate agreement on several appropriations bills—
including Transportation–HUD—appeared within reach. However, negotiations were derailed
by unrelated disputes, including issues surrounding presidential pardon authority. Congress


                                                                                                      23

recessed for the holidays on December 19 and will return on January 5, leaving just four
weeks to reach agreement before the CR expires.

As a reminder, the Senate FY26 Transportation, Housing, and Urban Development (THUD) bill
includes $68 million in capital and operating assistance for public transportation systems
supporting Olympic Games–related mobility needs. While the House bill does not include
funding for Olympic mobility, it does provide $750,000 in Community Project Funding
(earmarks) for Metrolink projects.

Metrolink Supports Cargo Theft Prevention Bill
Metrolink expressed support for S. 1404 / H.R. 2853, the Combating Organized Retail Crime
Act (CORCA) of 2025. The bipartisan legislation, introduced by Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
and Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV) in the Senate and Reps. David Joyce (R-OH) and Susie
Lee (D-NV) in the House, aims to reduce freight rail theft, thereby improving on-time reliability
for all rail operators. Specifically, the bill expands criminal forfeiture, money laundering
authorities, and the ability to aggregate thefts across supply chains. It also establishes a
dedicated coordination center within the Department of Homeland Security to align law
enforcement and industry efforts. The bicameral, bipartisan proposal is supported by the
Association of American Railroads (AAR) and the Intermodal Association of North America
(IANA), among others.

SUBJECT:                  Contract No. C3157R-26 - Fire Alarm and Switchgear
                          Replacement Project - Recommendation to Award - Golden
                          Phoenix Construction


Issue

The Authority requires the removal and replacement of the existing Fire Alarm System and
electrical switchgear at the Central Maintenance Facility (CMF), located at 1555 N. San
Fernando Road, Los Angeles, CA 90065. Both systems contain components that have
reached the end of their service life, frequently require repairs, or have otherwise become
obsolete, and must therefore be replaced to ensure safety, reliability, and compliance with
current standards.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the Board authorize the Chief Executive Officer to award Contract No.
C3157R-26 Fire Alarm and Switchgear Replacement Project to the lowest responsive and
responsible bidder, Golden Phoenix Construction in the amount of $1,687,050, consisting of
the bid amount of $1,467,000 plus a 15% contingency of $220,050.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan Commitments of:

      Safety Is Foundational: Replacing aging fire alarm and switchgear infrastructure
      enhances the safety and security of Metrolink employees and facilities by improving
      detection, notification, and electrical reliability.

      Modernizing Business Practices: This project advances state of good repair goals by



                                                                                                    76

      replacing obsolete systems with modern, maintainable, and code-compliant equipment,
      increasing operational efficiency and reducing unplanned outages.


Background

Contract No. C3157R-26 will replace the fire alarm and electrical switchgear at the CMF, two
critical systems ensuring safe and reliable operation of the facility. The existing condition of
each of these systems are explained in more detail below.

Fire Alarm Replacement
The existing fire alarm system at the CMF no longer meets current code and technology
standards. This project will replace the existing system with a modern, addressable fire alarm
and voice evacuation system in accordance with applicable National Fire Protection
Association (NFPA) requirements. All construction activities will occur while the CMF remains
fully operational. This necessitates a carefully managed execution plan with defined phases,
precise scheduling, and close coordination with SCRRA Operations and Facilities staff.

Switchboard Replacement
The CMF is served by a primary electrical distribution system that provides power to critical
facility operations. The existing electrical switchboards have reached the end of their expected
service life and require replacement to support continued safe and reliable operation of the
facility. The scope of work includes the replacement of the facility’s primary electrical
switchboards and associated electrical infrastructure necessary to support long-term
operational needs.


Discussion

On August 22, 2025, Staff issued an Invitation for Bids (IFB) for the Fire Alarm & Switchgear
Replacement Project for a contract term of 540 calendar days after the Notice to Proceed
(NTP) date. The solicitation was posted on the Authority's solicitation system and advertised
in publications in the five-member counties. Notices were also sent directly to firms registered
in the Authority's online vendor database. Fifty-three firms downloaded the solicitation.
Representatives from two interested firms attended the pre-bid meeting and the job walk
conducted on September 5, 2025. Four (4) bids were received on the due date of November
7, 2025. This procurement is a rebid of a February 2025 solicitation in which the apparent low
bidder was found to be non-responsive due to non-compliance with FTA DBE requirements
(49 CFR Part 26).

Budget Impact

The amounts for which contract authority is requested are included in the adopted Capital
Budget for FY20, FY23, and FY24.
