Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:
      Modernizing Business Practices: We will improve our operational efficiency through
      transparency, objective metrics and streamlined governance, reducing over-reliance on
      subsidy while bringing our system into a state of good repair and investing in the
      development of our employees. The report provides our Board with timely updates on
      the progress of the Capital Program. The new capital program, including SCORE, adds
      to the safety, expansion, and growth of the system while the State of Good Repair
      Program ensures the safety and reliability of the Authority’s existing assets.


Background

The Capital Program consists of two major components: New Capital Projects and State of
Good Repair (SoGR) Programs. The Authority’s Capital Program, outside of SCORE, is
budgeted annually, and projects are typically delivered over multiple years. Funding for capital



                                                                                                      144

projects is provided by Member Agencies through the annual budget process. The Authority
also applies for local, state, and federal funds for additional SoGR and New Capital Projects.

New Capital Projects expand railroad infrastructure and improve the customer experience,
including items such as new sidings, safety enhancements to grade crossings, modernizing
signal and communication systems, and new rolling stock.

The SoGR Program addresses existing capital assets to keep them in a state of good repair
through activities such as:
     Rehabilitation of tunnels, bridges, and culverts
     Replacement of worn ties and rail
     Replacement of worn or outdated signal system components
     Programmed rehabilitation of rolling stock components such as car door operators and
     heating/ventilation/air conditioning (HVAC), and mid-life overhaul of rail cars and
     locomotives

All project progress is tracked through the Authority’s project reporting system, which is
maintained by the Program Management Oversight (PMO) department. Regular meetings are
held with project managers to review the progress of active projects. Staff also prepare
quarterly project expenditure forecasts to estimate cash flow requirements. As part of the
PMO’s effort to improve its reporting and tracking capabilities, key performance indicators
(KPIs) have been developed and are included in this report.

This item has been updated to reflect financial expenditures and project status through
September 30, 2025.


Discussion

Since the last Capital Program Status Update in October 2025, multiple key accomplishments
were achieved, as follows:

SCORE Program:
   Received approval from the California Transportation Commission (CTC) for
   construction allocation for Marengo project during their August board meeting. We are
   waiting for the supplement paperwork to be officially provided to Metrolink.
   Requested supplemental funding allocation from CTC to complete Camera Ready
   design for the El Monte Siding Project.
   Continuing negotiations with the City of El Monte on the Purchase & Sale Agreement on
   the El Monte Siding project.
   Negotiations with Union Pacific Railroad regarding relocation of fiber-optic lines for the
   Simi Valley Double Track Project are ongoing.
   Requested construction funding allocation for the Rancho Cucamonga project.
   Development of the Invitation for Bids (IFB) for the San Gabriel Sub projects (Marengo
   Siding and Rancho Cucamonga Siding) continues.
   Requested supplemental funding allocation from CTC to complete condemnation for the
   Chatsworth Pedestrian Underpass Project.

Program Delivery has finished construction and completed our Early Start projects which
came in around $11M under budget. The team is working towards the construction of


                                                                                                 145

Metrolink-Led SCORE projects for which the design is nearing completion. With substantial
completion of design, the team has a better forecast for ROW acquisitions and utility
relocations that are needed for each of these projects and their associated costs. Due to
substantial completion of design for Metrolink-Led SCORE projects the team has high
confidence in the cost estimates for ROW acquisitions, utility relocations and construction.
There is estimated to be a funding gap, totaling approximately $300M for construction projects
due to inflation and material cost and general construction cost escalations seen since the
pandemic and combined with higher-than-expected ROW acquisition and utility relocation
needs and associated costs. It should be noted that budgets for Metrolink-Led SCORE
projects were established prior to the onset of the pandemic.

Authority staff have been collaborating with our funding partners at CalSTA, Caltrans, and the
Member Agencies to determine strategies to address the funding gap and advance key
projects. These strategies include prioritizing projects based on operational benefits,
reallocation of available funds from projects that have been completed under budget or that
have been deferred and pursuing additional grant funding opportunities.

State of Good Repair Program:
     On-Board Train Control Systems Rehabilitation:
          Train Management Computer (TMC) Upgrade: 132 out of 140 units have been
          upgraded. Estimate time of completion to upgrade remaining units is
          February 2026.
          Global Positioning System Upgrade: Models selected for pilot installations are
          completed with new hardware. Upgrade process to take approximately 2 years on
          all operational units.
          Next Gen Data Radios: Procurement of new Data Radios pending Meteorcomm
          rollout plan.
          PTC Simulators: The purchase order for the two new simulators has been
          processed, as well as the purchase order for the CGI upgrade to the existing
          simulator.

     Rolling Stock State of Good Repair:
           Rotem HVAC Overhaul: 134 of 136 HVAC units overhauled; 50/68 control panels
           overhauled.
           Bombardier HVAC Overhaul: Initial order of 180 units overhauled; Additional order
           of 87 HVACs to be overhauled has been placed and 41 of 87 units overhauled.

     SoGR Track, Structures, & Signal Projects by Line:
         Antelope Valley Line
              Structures design – Valley Sub Structures design was kicked off, and design
              is expected to progress to 30% by next quarter.
              Tunnel 25 - 100% Design complete for Tunnel 25 tie/ballast rehab (FY23)
              Signal Construction – Construction in-progress with anticipated completion
              by June 2026 for projects funded in FY 2021-22.
              Track Rehab – Design finalized for projects funded in FY 2024-25.
              Scheduled to go out for bid by March 2026.

     Ventura County Line
          Pacific Surfliner Corridor Rehabilitation and Reliability Project: 100% Design
          Complete. Work completion planned for 2028.

Contract Expiration Performance Audit                                            2025-04-IA


                                        INTRODUCTION

The Internal Audit Department conducted the Contract Expiration Performance Audit
(Project #2025-04-IA). This audit was included in the Fiscal Year 2025 Internal Audit Plan
approved by the Board of Directors.

                                        BACKGROUND

The Authority manages a large portfolio of contracts that support operations, capital
projects, and grant-funded activities. A key control supporting management of this
portfolio is the Contract Status Report, an internally generated report produced weekly
from Oracle data. The report highlights both active and expired contracts and is
distributed to Agency staff responsible for the contracts listed. It serves as a monitoring
tool to assist with tracking contract funding status, expiration dates, and other key
information necessary for effective oversight.

As of June 16, 2025, the Contract Status Report listed approximately 2,900 contracts
tracked in the expired contracts tab. These documents include Blanket Purchase
Agreements, Contract Purchase Agreements, and Standard Purchase Orders, as
reflected in the Oracle R12 financial system, which serves as the Authority’s primary
platform for contract tracking, monitoring, and reporting.

Because of the size and complexity of this portfolio, it is critical that contracts are
managed properly and that effective controls are in place. Allowing services to continue
under expired contracts increases the risk of problematic spending, weakens compliance
with procurement policies and federal requirements, and reduces transparency for
management and the Board. It also creates potential legal risks, as the enforceability of
contract terms may be compromised once a contract has expired, making it more difficult
to defend the Authority if disputes arise. Strong contract oversight further ensures that
funding tied to projects or grants is released in a timely manner, supporting accurate
budgeting, timely project delivery, and compliance with grant obligations.

                    OBJECTIVES, SCOPE, AND METHODOLOGY
                                         OBJECTIVES

The objective of this audit was to evaluate the adequacy and effectiveness of controls
designed to prevent the use of contracts beyond their authorized term and to ensure
proper contract management procedures are followed.

                                           SCOPE

The scope of this audit focused on expired contracts identified in the Contract Status
Report dated June 16, 2025, which served as the primary population for testing. These
contracts included agreements with start dates as early as April 2012 and end dates
through June 2025. Internal Audit performed detailed testing on a selection of 25



                                             1
                                                                                              69

Contract Expiration Performance Audit                                            2025-04-IA


contracts from the report, as well as a judgmental sample of five additional contracts, to
evaluate amendment timing and system enforcement of expiration dates.

                                        METHODOLOGY

To accomplish the audit objectives, Internal Audit:

      Reviewed key guidance:
           o CPMM policies/SOPs (CP-01 Sole Source, CP-02 Amendments, CP-04
               Closeout, PA3.02 Procurement Manual).
           o Green Book (GAO-25-107721, May 2025): Standards for Internal Control in
               the Federal Government, emphasizing timely and accurate execution of
               control activities.
           o Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR): Requirements for full and open
               competition (FAR 6.101), limitations on contracting without competition
               (FAR 6.301), exceptions for sole source (FAR 6.302), and timing of option
               exercises (FAR 17.204).
      Obtained weekly Contract Status Reports, using the June 16, 2025 report (active
       and expired tabs) as the primary population.
      Compared Contract Status Report data to CPMM contract files and Oracle records;
       interviewed/corresponded with CPMM, Project Managers, and IT regarding
       accuracy, use, and distribution.
      Examined contracts, amendments, memos, and supporting documentation from
       CPMM’s secure drive; verified amendment timing, routing, and approvals.
      Tested Oracle controls by reviewing invoices and PO activity, and confirmed
       system enforcement and manual workarounds with CPMM/IT.
      Reviewed 25 contracts from the June 16, 2025 report plus 5 judgmentally selected
       contracts (EN109RB-20, L176-21, SP504R-20, E745C-20, and the E742 series).


We conducted this performance audit in accordance with generally accepted government
auditing standards and in conformance with Global Internal Audit Standards promulgated
by the Institute of Internal Auditors. Those standards require that we plan and perform the
audit to obtain sufficient and appropriate evidence to provide a reasonable basis for our
findings and conclusions based on our audit objectives. We believe that the evidence
obtained provides a reasonable basis for our findings and conclusions based on our audit
objectives.

                                        CONCLUSION

Overall, Internal Audit found that the Authority's contract management processes for
expired contracts have improved with key controls through Contract Status Report and
Oracle system. The weekly Contract Status Report provides visibility into both active and
expired contracts; while its content and distribution can be improved, its existence
demonstrates a proactive approach to oversight. In addition, CPMM has shown initiative




                                             2
                                                                                              70

Contract Expiration Performance Audit                                           2025-04-IA


by beginning the amendment process prior to expiration and obtaining Board approval
before contracts lapsed, even though final signatures were sometimes delayed.
That said, improvements are still needed in timeliness, documentation, and monitoring as
outlined in this report. Addressing these areas (while continuing to build on the positive
practices already in place) will strengthen the Authority’s ability to manage contracts
effectively. Leveraging the upcoming Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM) system
offers an opportunity to modernize reporting, improve consistency, and reinforce
compliance with policy and regulatory requirements.

                                    REVIEW OF REPORT

Management has reviewed and agrees with the audit findings and recommendations in
this report and has developed a corrective action plan to address the recommendations.

Internal Audit thanks the Contract, Procurement and Materials Management Department
for their assistance and cooperation during our audit.

If you have any questions or comments, please contact Elisabeth Lazuardi, Director of
Audit at (213) 452-0335 or LazuardiE@scrra.net.




                                            3
                                                                                             71

Contract Expiration Performance Audit                                          2025-04-IA


      OBSERVATIONS, RECOMMENDATIONS, AND MANAGEMENT
                        RESPONSES

Finding 1 Contract Amendments executed after Expiration Date

Criteria
CPMM SOP CP-02 (Contract Amendments) states that “expired contracts cannot be
modified,” establishing that amendments must be executed before a contract’s expiration
date.

Condition
Internal Audit identified four contracts (out of 30 total contracts tested) (EN109RB-20,
L176-21, SP504R-20, and E745C-20) where amendments were executed after the
contract expiration date, contrary to CPMM SOP CP-02, which states that “expired
contracts cannot be modified.” In each case, the intent of both parties to amend was
established prior to expiration (through Board approval or routing initiation), but final
signatures were not obtained until after the contract had lapsed.

Internal Audit noted the following:
    All required signatures were not obtained prior to the expiration date.
    Although intent to continue services was in place, delays created periods when the
      Authority lacked a fully executed contract.
    Discussion with General Counsel revealed that while these cases may not be
      “fatal,” they weaken the Authority’s legal position in disputes, create compliance
      risks, and may reduce transparency if delays are not disclosed to the Board.

Cause
Amendment delays were primarily due to staff turnover, communication breakdowns, and
lack of process controls to ensure timely execution. Another contributing factor is SOP
CP-02 which only states amendments must be executed before a contract’s expiration
date but does not explicitly state that all signatures are required before the expiration
date.

Effect

Executing amendments after contract expiration creates compliance concerns, weakens
enforceability in disputes, and can give the appearance of sole source contracting when
services continue without a written agreement. It also reduces transparency for the Board
if gaps in the terms of an agreement are not disclosed.




                                           4
                                                                                            72

Contract Expiration Performance Audit                                       2025-04-IA


Recommendation

1. Revise SOP CP-02 to clearly state that all amendments must be signed by all parties
   before contract expiration.
2. Implement a process to ensure continuity when Contract Administrators (CA) leave,
   including a review of contracts they manage to identify upcoming expirations and
   needed amendments.
3. Factor these issues in the scope of the new contract management system, considering
   features such as:
   o Automated alerts and dashboards (e.g.,180, 150, 120 etc… day reminders before
       expiration).
   o Routing visibility to track amendment progress.
   o Automatic updates to routing status report to current Project Managers.

Management Response

Agree

Corrective Action Plan

   1. Revise SOP CP-02 to clearly state that all amendments must be signed by all
      parties before contract expiration.
   2. As part of the off-boarding process, the Manager will review the CA workload and
      determine if the CA is working on amending an expired contract. If so, they will
      assign a new CA to complete the amendment. The CLM system will assist with
      this requirement, in the short term, we can enter an IPG during the mid-year
      performance review.
   3. Factor these features in the scope of the new contract management system,
      considering features such as:
        o Automated alerts and dashboards (e.g.,180, 150, 120 etc… day reminders
           before expiration).
        o Routing visibility to track amendment progress.
        o Automatic updates to routing status report to current Project Managers.

   Target Implementation Date
   1. December 31, 2025
   2. January 31, 2026
   3. June 30, 2027
   Responsible for Implementation
   1. Cynthia Minix, Director CPMM
   2. Angelos Kastrisianakis, Senior Manager Contracts & Compliance
      Cynthia Minix, Director CPMM
   3. Cynthia Minix, Director CPMM




                                          5
                                                                                         73

Contract Expiration Performance Audit                                               2025-04-IA


   Accountable for Implementation
   1. Tom Schamber, CFO
   2. Tom Schamber, CFO
   3. Tom Schamber, CFO

Finding 2 – Contract Status Report: Accuracy and Distribution

Criteria

Green Book Principle 13.02 Management designs a process that uses the entity’s
objectives and related risks to identify the information requirements needed to support
the internal control system. Information requirements consider the needs of both internal
and external users. Management defines the identified information requirements at the
relevant level and requisite specificity for appropriate personnel.
Condition

Internal Audit reviewed the June 16, 2025, Contract Status Report, a weekly Oracle R12-
generated report distributed to Project Managers to monitor contract activity. The report
includes tabs for active and expired contracts and provides data such as contract
amounts, dates, Project Manager assignments, and funding status.

The Contract Status Report is the Authority’s only centralized monitoring report for
contracts, making it the primary tool management and Project Managers rely on to track
contract status across the agency. Because of its central role, it is critical that the report
be both accurate and consistently distributed. Any weaknesses in content or distribution
limit management’s ability to effectively oversee the agency’s contract portfolio.

Testing of 30 contracts reflected in the report and supporting contract files, along with
interviews with CPMM, IT, and Project Managers, identified weaknesses in two primary
areas: Report Content and Report Distribution.

I. Report Content
   The Contract Status Report is intended to provide management with a reliable view of
   the Authority’s contract portfolio; however, testing revealed several issues affecting its
   accuracy and clarity. Some contracts were shown with incorrect or inconsistent
   expiration dates, while others were inconsistently classified due to differences between
   Oracle’s procurement categories and CPMM’s definitions. In addition, certain non-
   contract items (e.g., credit lines, or short-term leases) appeared on the report as if they
   were contracts, which further reduces its usefulness as a monitoring tool. Below are
   issues noted per audit testing.

       Expiration Date Discrepancies: Testing reflected an instance where the
        expiration date displayed in the Contract Status Report did not match the actual
        contract terms, creating confusion about whether agreements were still valid.
        MU124-12A, a mutual aid and refueling Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)


                                              6
                                                                                                 74

Contract Expiration Performance Audit                                              2025-04-IA


        with NCTD, does not have a defined expiration date according to CPMM, yet it
        was still listed on the report. The Oracle entry was created to facilitate payment
        tracking between the agencies, not to represent a contract requiring monitoring.
        CPMM noted that MOUs of this type are not typically tracked as part of contract
        administration and indicated a need to review how many MOUs currently appear
        on the Contract Status Report to determine whether they should continue to be
        included.
       Contracts Classification Consistency: Internal Audit noted inconsistencies
        between how contracts and procurements are classified in Oracle R12 compared
        to CPMM’s policies and SOPs. The “Type” column in the Contract Status Report
        (CSR) currently pulls from the Oracle document header, which identifies
        document form (e.g., Contract, Blanket PO, Standard PO), whereas the
        procurement type (e.g., Sole Source, IFB, RFP, Cooperative/Piggyback) is stored
        in the flex field. This structure limits reporting visibility and can cause Oracle-
        generated reports to misrepresent certain procurements as “contracts,” even
        when CPMM does not consider them contractual agreements. The flex field,
        however, contains the appropriate procurement type and could be used to
        enhance the accuracy and specificity of CSR reporting.

        In addition, audit testing identified other financial arrangements that are not truly
        contracts but still appear in the report, such as lease agreements, warranty
        tracking and informal Oracle credit lines. These items further reduce the accuracy
        and clarity of the report. Examples from the Contract Status Report include:

           o MTL1400578: Reflected as a Standard PO, but this was a one-time IT
                purchase order from 2013.
           o X1300181: Reflected as a Standard PO, but this was a short-term lease
                arrangement.
       Multi-year agreements structured as annual agreements: Contract OP151-22
        was set up in Oracle as separate annual headers (e.g., OP151-22-23), rather than
        a single multi-year contract. This fragmented approach makes it difficult to track
        the full contract authority and can create confusion when reviewing the report.
       Old inactive contracts: Contracts dating back as far as 2013 remain on the
        expired tab. Retaining such old items adds unnecessary volume and reduces the
        report’s usability as a monitoring tool.
       Data Discrepancies & Support: Contract PO919 - the Contract Status Report
        reflected the contracted amount at $375,000, but the executed amendment and
        Oracle award reflected $500,000. Documentation in the CPMM drive had not been
        updated to reflect the amendment. CPMM has since corrected the discrepancy
        in Oracle and updated supporting documentation prior to finalization of this report.

  These issues collectively reduce the accuracy and reliability of the Contract Status
  Report as a monitoring tool.

II. Report Distribution



                                              7
                                                                                                75

Contract Expiration Performance Audit                                              2025-04-IA


  The report is not consistently distributed. Some Project Managers never received it,
  while others listed had already left the Agency. IT only updates the distribution list upon
  request and does not oversee its accuracy. No department owns the list, creating
  accountability gaps.

Cause
Continuous staff turnover and insufficient coordination between CPMM, IT, and Project
Managers have contributed to the lack of development of consistent definitions and
reliable reporting. Contract type definitions in Oracle are not fully aligned with CPMM
classifications, leading to inappropriate classifications. Report distribution lacks clear
ownership.
Effect
These weaknesses reduce the accuracy and reliability of the Contract Status Report.
Inappropriately classified contracts, outdated contracts, and gaps in distribution
undermine its usefulness as a monitoring tool. As a result, expired contracts may not be
consistently tracked, closed, or managed in a timely manner increasing the risk of
mismanagement, delayed closeouts, and reduced transparency.
Recommendation

4. CPMM should coordinate with IT and Project Managers to strengthen monitoring and
   reporting processes. Specific actions include:
      a) Change source of information on the Contract Status Report to the flex field
          that contains more detailed information.
      b) Establish clear ownership and oversight of the report distribution list so it
          remains current and accurate.
      c) Close completed contracts and remove them from the expired tab to improve
          usability and focus monitoring efforts on current items.

   Management Response
   Agree

Corrective Action Plan
  4a. Change source of information on the Contract Status Report to the flex field that
     contains the specific procurement type. This functionality in Oracle is being tested
     and must be moved to production before the report can be updated.

  4b. Establish clear ownership and oversight of the report distribution list so that it
     remains current and accurate. CPMM will be responsible for updating the Contract
     Administrator column and working with IDTS to keep the report distribution list
     current. The CA will update PMs in the Oracle system as they receive items to
     process.

  4c. Close completed contracts and remove them from the expired tab to improve
      usability and focus monitoring efforts on current items. Work with IDTS to close



                                             8
                                                                                                76

Contract Expiration Performance Audit                                         2025-04-IA


       expired POs that do not require the formal close out process initiated by Project
       Managers.

   Target Implementation Date
   4a. March 31, 2026
   4b. June 30, 2026
   4c. June 30, 2027
   Responsible for Implementation
   4a. Angelos Kastrisianakis, Senior Manager Contracts & Compliance
       Cynthia Minix, Director CPMM
   4b. Cynthia Minix, Director CPMM
   4c. Angelos Kastrisianakis, Senior Manager Contracts & Compliance
       Cynthia Minix, Director CPMM
   Accountable for Implementation
   4a. Tom Schamber, CFO
   4b. Tom Schamber, CFO
   4c. Tom Schamber, CFO
   Additional Management Note:

   As CPMM scopes the new Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM) system, these
   issues should be factored into the requirements to strengthen reporting accuracy,
   distribution reliability, and long-term monitoring practices - FY27/28.




                                           9
                                                                                           77

Contract Expiration Performance Audit                       2025-04-IA


Reviewed and acknowledged by:


                                        November 20, 2025
Darren M. Kettle,                        Date
Chief Executive Officer

matters.text:
B.   CONFERENCE WITH LABOR NEGOTIATOR – Pursuant to Government Code Section
     54957.6
     Agency Designated Representative: Chair Doug Chaffee
     Unrepresented Employee: Director, Internal Audit

C.   CONFERENCE WITH LEGAL COUNSEL – ANTICIPATED LITIGATION – Pursuant to
     Government Code Section 54956.9(d)(2) – one case

     The Board recessed at 10:38 a.m. to discuss Items 11.A – 11.C and reconvened at 11:40
     a.m. at which time Counsel indicated there was nothing to report.

12. CONSENT CALENDAR

12.A Approval of Meeting Minutes - September 26, 2025 Regular Board Meeting

     The Board (11-0) approved the Minutes of the September 26, 2025 Regular Board
     Meeting.

12.B Proposed Amendments to the Agency's Classification and Salary Plan

     Board approval is needed of proposed amendments to the Agency’s Classification and
     Salary Plan, in accordance with HR Policy No. 2.1.

     The Board (11-0) amended the Agency's Classification and Salary Plan and adopted it by
     resolution.

     There will be no budget impact because of these changes to the Classification and Salary
     Plan.

12.C Contract No. EP245-25 - MP36 Locomotive Service Life Extension and Repair -
     Recommendation to Award - Higher Power Industries (HPI)

     In an effort to provide robust service for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games and
     ensure a general state of good repair for the Authority's rolling stock fleet, the Authority
     intends to repair and overhaul four (4) out-of-service MP36 locomotives as a base order
     with this contract. In addition, the Authority may choose to overhaul up to eleven (11)
     additional in-service MP36 locomotives as an option order with this contract. In order to
     ensure effective use of public funds, overall fleet planning (including any potential new
     locomotive procurement) would be taken into consideration before exercising any life-
     extension overhaul options.

     The Board (11-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and execute Contract
     No. EP245-25 for MP36 Locomotive Service Life Extension and Repair, to Higher Power
     Industries (HPI) in the amount of $31,337,683.95 ($9,342,064.42 for the base order of 4
     locomotives and $21,995,619.53 for an option order of up to 11 locomotives) plus 20%
     contingency in the amount of $6,267,536.79 ($1,868,412.88 for the base and
     $4,399,123.91 combined for the Option) for total contract authorization amount, not- to-
     exceed $37,605,220.74. This award is subject to resolution of any timely filed protests.




                                               6
                                                                                                    13

    Contract amount for base order is $9,342,064.42, plus 20% contingency, a total of
    $11,210,477.30. The base order is included in FY23, FY24 and FY25 Capital Budgets
    adopted by the SCRRA Board of Directors, which totals $11,952,000 in available budget
    for this contract.

    Capital Budget for the option orders will be requested in future fiscal year Capital Budget
    cycles as needed. No funds will be spent without prior budget approval.

12.D Contract No. PO857-21 - Brake Pads and Shoes for Locomotive and Rail Cars -
     Recommendation to Increase Contract Authority - Railroad Friction Products
     Corporation

    The Materials Management Department utilizes contract PO857- 21 to purchase the Brake
    pads and shoes required to support maintenance of the Authority's rolling stock.

    The Board (11-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to increase the authority of Contract
    No. PO857- 21 with Railroad Friction Products Corporation by $350,000 for a new not-to-
    exceed total amount of $1,850,000.

    The amount for which contract authority is requested is included in the operating budget of
    the Materials Management Department for FY26.

12.E Sole Source Contract EP250-26 with Progress Rail Locomotive Inc and Single
     Source Contract EP251-26 with Quinn Power Systems for Procurement of
     Locomotive Parts and Repair Services for Maintenance of Locomotive Fleet

    The Authority's Materials Management Department is seeking approval to negotiate a multi
    -year sole source contract with Progress Rail Locomotive Inc and a multi-year single
    source contract with Quinn Power Systems to allow for the purchase of new parts and for
    repair services needed to perform maintenance of the Authority's locomotive fleet.

    The Board (11-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and award:
    1. A three-year term Sole Source Contract with Progress Rail Locomotive Inc. for the
       procurement of new parts and repair and return services for an estimated not-to-exceed
       amount of $8,000,000; and
    2. A three-year term Single Source Contract with Quinn Power Systems Inc for the
       procurement of new parts and repair and return services for an estimated amount not-
       to-exceed $6,500,000.

    For FY26 the contract authority requested will be $1,600,000 for Progress Rail Locomotive,
    and $1,000,000 for Quinn Power Systems. These amounts are included in the FY26
    operating budget for the Materials Management department. Funds needed for
    subsequent fiscal years will be requested through the annual budget process.

12.F Single Source Purchase Order No. EP248-26 - 20-Ton Rail Jacks for ZEMU -
     Recommendation to Award - BBM Railway Equipment, LLC

    The Authority requires a set of 20-ton portable jacks to accommodate the new Stadler Zero
    Emission Multiple Unit (ZEMU). The current jacks at Arrow Maintenance Facility are rated
    for 15-tons and were procured for the Stadler Diesel Multiple Unit (DMU) vehicles that

                                              7
                                                                                                    14

    SBCTA procured. The new ZEMU vehicle is heavier than the DMU and requires higher
    rated jacks for support.

    The Board (11-0) authorized the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and award the
    purchase of one set of 12 20-ton jacks, plus one spare to BBM Railway Equipment, LLC for
    a total not-to-exceed amount of $591,611.96.

    The amounts for which contract authority is requested are included in the Adopted Arrow
    Capital Budgets for FY2025 ($591,611.96).

12.G FY 2025 Internal Quality Assessment

    The Internal Audit Department (Internal Audit) completed the FY 2025 Internal Quality
    Assessment for the period of July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025.

    The Board received and filed this report.

12.H Capital Program Status Report

    Staff is providing an update on the Authority's Capital Program, including the Southern

SUBJECT:                  Amended Bylaws to Reflect New Governance Structure


Issue

At the September 2025 meeting, the Board approved, in principle, certain changes to the
Authority governance structure and directed Staff to present conforming edits to the Authority
Bylaws. Staff has completed the proposed changes (the “Amended Bylaws”) and presents
them to the Board for its consideration.

Recommendation

Executive Committee recommended (4-0) the Board approve the proposed Amended Bylaws
to become effective January 1, 2026.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Modernizing Business Practices: We will improve our operational efficiency through
      transparency, objective metrics and streamlined governance, reducing over-reliance on
      subsidy while bringing our system into a state of good repair and investing in the
      development of our employees. Amending the Authority’s Bylaws ensures that the
      governing documents provide an effective and efficient governance structure.


Discussion

The current Authority Bylaws provide for three standing committees consisting of:
  1. The Executive Committee (ECOM)



                                                                                                    7

  2. The Audit & Finance Committee (AFCOM)
  3. The Contracts, Operations, Maintenance & Safety Committee (COMS).

The proposed Amended Bylaws now before the Board would eliminate all three standing
committees and retain a single, monthly Board meeting.

In addition to the elimination of the three standing committees (see Section 5.0) and
references thereto, other notable changes reflected in the Amended Bylaws, based on the
Board motion and discussion, are as follows:
      The establishment and use of a consent calendar is retained in the Amended Bylaws by
      the Chair working in consultation with the CEO.
      The Amended Bylaws results in the elimination of Exhibit B to the Bylaws, which set forth
      the subject matter jurisdiction of each standing committee. (Exhibit A, the longstanding
      voting rules for each member agency, is retained without alteration.)
      The deletion of duplicative Public Comment section 9.6.
      The Amended Bylaws would become effective on January 1, 2026.

Attached hereto is a redline version of the proposed Amended Bylaws illustrating the
suggested changes, as well as a “clean” version of the proposed Amended Bylaws.


Budget Impact

There is no budget impact to the adoption of the Amended Bylaws.

repair and overhaul four (4) out-of-service MP36 locomotives as a base order with this
contract. In addition, the Authority may choose to overhaul up to eleven (11) additional in-
service MP36 locomotives as an option order with this contract. In order to ensure effective
use of public funds, overall fleet planning (including any potential new locomotive
procurement) would be taken into consideration before exercising any life-extension overhaul
options.

Recommendation

Contracts, Operations, Maintenance, and Safety Committee recommended (3-0) the Board
authorize the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and execute Contract No. EP245-25 for
MP36 Locomotive Service Life Extension and Repair, to Higher Power Industries (HPI) in the
amount of $31,337,683.95 ($9,342,064.42 for the base order of 4 locomotives and
$21,995,619.53 for an option order of up to 11 locomotives) plus 20% contingency in the
amount of $6,267,536.79 ($1,868,412.88 for the base and $4,399,123.91 combined for the
Option) for total contract authorization amount, not-to-exceed $37,605,220.74. This award is
subject to resolution of any timely filed protests.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan Commitments of:



                                                                                                      102

     Safety is Foundational: We will stay on the leading edge by deploying new
     technologies and processes to enhance the safety and security of our riders, our fellow
     employees, and the communities we serve. This project will overhaul locomotives that
     are currently out-of-service, returning them to a condition safe for operation of revenue
     service.

     Customers Are Our Business: We respect and value our customers, putting them at
     the heart of all we do, and work hard to attract and retain new customers by
     understanding their needs and finding new and innovative ways to bring them on board.
     This project will provide more available equipment to support 2028 LA Olympic and
     Paralympic Games.


Background

The Authority owns a total of 60 locomotives, 15 of which are Tier 2 MP36 PH locomotives
that were delivered in 2008 and 2009. Of the 15 MP36 locomotives, 4 are currently out-of-
service (OOS) due to deferred maintenance and multiple component parts that are obsolete
and no longer available. The remaining 11 MP36 locomotives that are currently in service are
overdue for a mid-life overhaul to ensure reliable service.

The Authority is also pursuing grant opportunities to fund the replacement of up to 12 of these
Tier 2 MP36 locomotives with new Tier 4 locomotives. Assuming that funding is secured and
agreements with the grantors are executed in timely manner, the Authority's estimated delivery
timeline to receive new Tier 4 locomotives spans from mid-2030 to early-2032. Until the new
Tier 4 locomotives are received, the existing Tier 2 locomotives will be needed to provide
reliable service, necessitating that they are in a state of good repair.

As one of the key rehabilitation projects in the Olympic Readiness Program, this contract will
support the repair and overhaul the 4 OOS MP36 locomotives as a base order with an option
to overhaul up to 11 additional MP36 locomotives. The primary intent is to return the 4 OOS
locomotives to service to support the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games with maximum
number of available locomotives to provide the most robust service possible. The inclusion of
an option order to complete the overhaul of the remaining 11 MP36 locomotives provides
flexibility to the Authority to ensure that the MP36 fleet operates reliably until the new Tier 4
locomotives are procured and delivered. In order to ensure effective use of public funds, prior
to exercising any life-extension overhaul options, overall fleet planning will be considered,
including an assessment of each individual locomotive condition.


Discussion

On October 10, 2024, the Authority issued Request for Proposals (RFP) No. EP245-25 for the
Service Life Extension and repair of the MP36 locomotives. The RFP was posted on the
Authority's online procurement portal and notifications were sent to 1513 registered firms. The
Authority also advertised the RFP in publications in the five member counties and in diversity
newspapers. Forty-three prospective proposers viewed the RFP on the procurement portal, of
those only fifteen are classified as primes, the other twenty-eight are classified as sub-
contractors or suppliers. Four prospective proposers attended the virtual Pre-Proposal


                                                                                                    103

Conference held on October 15, 2024, and three firms attended the 2-day job walk on October
23 & 24, 2024. The Authority received and answered 73 questions.

The Authority received a single proposal from HPI by the submission date of February 20,
2025. Staff completed post-solicitation research of prospective proposers. It was concluded
that they lacked sufficient capacity and expertise to execute the project.

Negotiations with HPI began on August 19, 2025, to review the project assumptions,
availability of parts, the aggressive project schedule, and possible risks. During negotiation
discussions the obsolescence of parts and equipment for two major systems was identified as
a major risk. As a result, HPI proposed changes to address these risks, which required
additional work.

The final proposed price is above the independent cost estimate (ICE) as shown in the table
below:

Independent Cost Estimate                 $24,080,059.70
Final Proposed Price                      $31,337,683.95
+/-                                              30.14%


After reviewing the various factors and related risks to this contract the total of $31,337,683.95
for the repair and service life extension of 15 locomotives was found to be fair and reasonable
- $9,342,064.42 for the base order of 4 locomotives and $21,995,619.53 for the option orders
of 11 locomotives. This Contract is federally funded with a DBE goal of 3.0% which HPI is
required to meet.

Due to the nature of the work, Staff has included a contingency of 20% to cover out-of-scope
repairs, resulting in a total not-to-exceed contract authorization amount of $37,605,220.74.


Budget Impact

Contract amount for base order is $9,342,064.42, plus 20% contingency, a total of
$11,210,477.30. The base order is included in FY23, FY24 and FY25 Capital Budgets adopted
by the SCRRA Board of Directors, which totals $11,952,000 in available budget for this
contract.

Capital Budget for the option orders will be requested in future fiscal year Capital Budget
cycles as needed. No funds will be spent without prior budget approval.



Next Steps

Upon Board approval of the recommendation, Staff will execute a contract with HPI and issue
a Notice to Proceed.

Issue

The Materials Management Department utilizes contract PO857-21 to purchase the Brake
pads and shoes required to support maintenance of the Authority's rolling stock.

Recommendation

Contracts, Operations, Maintenance, and Safety Committee recommended (3-0) the Board to
authorize the Chief Executive Officer to increase the authority of Contract No. PO857- 21 with
Railroad Friction Products Corporation by $350,000 for a new not-to-exceed total amount of
$1,850,000.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Safety is Foundational: We will stay on the leading edge by deploying new
      technologies and processes to enhance the safety and security of our riders, our fellow
      employees, and the communities we serve. Replacement of brake pads and shoes are
      necessary to maintain the Authority's rolling stock in a state of good repair.


Background

The Authority's fleet of locomotives and passenger cars use brake pads and brake shoes to
stop its trains. A brake pad applies friction to the side of a wheel or brake rotor while a brake



                                                                                                      106

shoe applies friction to the wheel tread which contacts the rail. The Authority uses three types
of brake pads and three types of brake shoes to support its locomotives, Bombardier cars,
and Rotem cars. To ensure that the brake systems of the rolling stock fleet work properly, old
brake pads and shoes are replaced with new ones as they wear out.

On March 26, 2021, the Board approved the award of Contract No. PO857-21 - Brake Pads
and Shoes for Locomotives and Rail Cars to Friction Products Corporation for a three-year
base period and one two-year option for a not-to-exceed amount of $1,500,000. On April 1,
2024, the two-year option was exercised, and the Contract is set to expire on March 30, 2026.
Due to higher-than-expected usage, the original contract Authority has almost been
exhausted.


Discussion

The Authority utilizes Contract PO857-21 to purchase new brake pads and shoes needed to
ensure timely replacement of old worn brake and brake pads on its fleet of Locomotives and
Passenger cars. As seen in recent years prices for parts have seen a considerable increase.
A quick quote request to compare the pricing of the F125 Locomotive Brake Shoe model V330
against current pricing by other suppliers showed that by taking advantage of the pricing for
contract No. PO857-21 the Authority will see a savings of $20.44 for each brake shoe.

Brake Model                     Contract PO857-21 Pricing       Progress Rail's Quote
V330                            $15.50                          $35.94

A new IFB will be advertised in the coming months to replace PO857-21, but it is in the
Authority's best interest to continue taking advantage of the pricing under PO857-21
established five years ago.


Budget Impact

The amount for which contract authority is requested is included in the operating budget of the
Materials Management Department for FY26.


Next Steps

Upon approval by the Board, staff will continue issuing Purchase Orders on as-needed basis
to Railroad Friction Products to replenish inventory of brake shoes and brake pads.

Issue

The Authority's Materials Management Department is seeking approval to negotiate a multi-
year sole source contract with Progress Rail Locomotive Inc and a multi-year single source
contract with Quinn Power Systems to allow for the purchase of new parts and for repair
services needed to perform maintenance of the Authority's locomotive fleet.

Recommendation

Contracts, Operations, Maintenance, and Safety Committee recommended (3-0) the Board
authorize the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and award:
  1. A three-year term Sole Source Contract with Progress Rail Locomotive Inc. for the
     procurement of new parts and repair and return services for an estimated not-to-exceed
     amount of $8,000,000; and
  2. A three-year term Single Source Contract with Quinn Power Systems Inc for the
     procurement of new parts and repair and return services for an estimated amount not-to-
     exceed $6,500,000.


Strategic Commitment

The report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Customers Are Our Business: We respect and value our customers, putting them at
      the heart of all we do, and work hard to attract and retain new customers by



                                                                                                   108

     understanding their needs and finding new and innovative ways to delight them. This
     single source contract allows Metrolink the ability to purchase and maintain adequate
     inventory of the parts needed to support the timely maintenance of the Authority's
     Locomotive Fleets.


Background

Progress Rail Locomotive Inc. is the Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) of the Authority's
F125 Locomotives. It is also the main supplier for many of the components used by our
legacy fleets. Quinn Power Systems is the dealer authorized by Caterpillar to sell engine
components to the Authority. Caterpillar is the OEM of the C175-20 Engines that power our
F125 Locomotives and C-27 Engines which power our legacy fleets.

Currently the Authority purchases parts and repair and return services from Progress Rail
Locomotive and Quinn Power Systems on an as needed basis utilizing contract authority
approved by the Board each fiscal year through its annual budget request process. On June
27, 2025, the board approved annual contract authority of $3,500,000 for contract PO759 for
Progress Rail Locomotive Inc and $2,500,000 for contract PO409 for Quinn Power Systems
under Item 6.A, attachment L (Annual Contract Authority Renewal). The successful negotiation
of multi-year contract agreements with these suppliers will replace the yearly request brought
before the board for annual contract authority for these suppliers.


Discussion

Progress Rail Locomotive Inc is the Authority's main supplier for 340 one-time-use parts and
84 repairable parts, and Quinn Power Systems is the Authority's main supplier for 293 one
time-use-parts and 15 repairable parts for the maintenance of its locomotive fleets. By
establishing multi-year agreements with these suppliers, the Authority will be able to negotiate
favorable terms, shorter lead times, and lock in set pricing. This will allow for better forecasting
and improve availability of key components to support timely maintenance of the Locomotive
fleets.

In addition, establishing multi-year contracts will also streamline the procurement process and
significantly reduce purchase order processing times for orders from these suppliers. Instead
of requesting new quotes for every purchase order, these contracts will allow for the creation
of blanket purchase agreements within our ERP system. With pricing already set, the
procurement department will be able to process purchase orders in a more efficient and cost-
effective manner.


Budget Impact

For FY26 the contract authority requested will be $1,600,000 for Progress Rail Locomotive,
and $1,000,000 for Quinn Power Systems. These amounts are included in the FY26 operating
budget for the Materials Management department. Funds needed for subsequent fiscal years
will be requested through the annual budget process.




                                                                                                       109

Next Steps

Upon approval of this request, staff will negotiate pricing with Progress Rail Locomotive Inc
and Quinn Power Systems for three-year agreements for new parts and repair services that
will be awarded by the CEO.

SUBJECT:                  Single Source Purchase Order No. EP248-26 - 20-Ton Rail
                          Jacks for ZEMU - Recommendation to Award - BBM Railway
                          Equipment, LLC


Issue

The Authority requires a set of 20-ton portable jacks to accommodate the new Stadler Zero
Emission Multiple Unit (ZEMU). The current jacks at Arrow Maintenance Facility are rated for
15-tons and were procured for the Stadler Diesel Multiple Unit (DMU) vehicles that SBCTA
procured. The new ZEMU vehicle is heavier than the DMU and requires higher rated jacks for
support.

Recommendation

Contracts, Operations, Maintenance, and Safety Committee recommended (3-0) the Board
authorize the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and award the purchase of one set of 12 20-
ton jacks, plus one spare to BBM Railway Equipment, LLC for a total not-to-exceed amount of
$591,611.96.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Safety is Foundational: We will stay on the leading edge by deploying new
      technologies and processes to enhance the safety and security of our riders, our fellow
      employees, and the communities we serve. The new jacks will support vehicle
      maintenance for both the ZEMU and the DMUs at AMF to perform required preventative
      and corrective maintenance.




                                                                                                    111

Background

On December 2024, an on-call Work Directive (WD) RFP was issued to Stadler US, Inc. under
contract MS337-25, to procure portable jacks on the Authority’s behalf. The WD RFP was
issued to Stadler requesting a cost proposal by January 13, 2025. After a 6-month delay and
several follow-ups by staff, Stadler obtained four quotes and provided a cost proposal on June
5, with a 20% profit markup. After several negotiation meetings between the Authority and
Stadler, the profit markup was lowered, with 15% being the lowest profit margin that Stadler
was willing to accept for this or any future on-call requests. SBCTA, who funds this contract,
did not accept Stadler’s 15% profit markup. Staff raised concerns about a prohibited “cost plus
percentage of cost” approach and creating a precedent of excessive profit for future requests.

Of the four quotes that Stadler provided, two are above the budget available for the lift jacks.
The lowest bid received is from RailQuip, Inc., the firm that provided the current jacks to the
Authority and has demonstrated continued deficiencies providing support services and
maintenance for the jacks already in-service. Support is also impacted by long lead time and
high delivery costs for spare parts from Europe. Therefore, staff does not recommend
procuring additional lift jacks from this vendor.


Discussion

To maintain and repair the heavier newly acquired Stadler ZEMU vehicles, higher capacity
jacks are required. ZEMU vehicles weigh 123.6 tons compared to DMU's 114-ton weight,
which requires a minimum of 18-ton jacks instead of the 15-ton currently in service. The
proposed 20-ton jacks will accommodate heavier ZEMU train sets with additional 2-ton
capacity for safety. The procurement includes a set of 12 jacks, a control panel, and one
additional spare jack.

Separate approval will be obtained by SBCTA to authorize disposal of the old jacks at a
surplus auction.

Due to the delay in the process the Authority is requesting a single-source approval to
expedite delivery of the jack set to meet service requirements for the ZEMU. There are only a
handful of vendors capable of delivering jacks to the Authority within the available budget and
dimensions required. The Authority is recommending BBM Railway Equipment, LLC because
of its established US presence and availability of post-delivery support. Aside from the current
supplier of jacks, other vendors are priced substantially higher than BBM.

Below is a summary of quotes received for jack vendors:

            Supplier                                 Quoted Price
            RailQuip, Inc.                           $529,437.50
            BBM Railway Equipment LLC                $544,000
            Whiting Corporation                      $818,085
            Garcia Machinery                         $1,116,000
            Stadler WD Price Proposal                $654,615.26 (20% profit)
                                                     $627,339.63 (15% profit,
            Stadler WD Price Proposal                post-negotiation)


                                                                                                   112

Budget Impact

The amounts for which contract authority is requested are included in the Adopted Arrow
Capital Budgets for FY2025 ($591,611.96).


Next Steps

Upon Board approval, staff will negotiate a single source agreement with BBM Railway
Equipment, LLC. Upon successful completion of the negotiations, the Authority will issue
Purchase Order EP248-26 for a total not-to-exceed amount of $591,611.96, which includes
sales tax.

SUBJECT:                  FY 2025 Internal Quality Assessment


Issue

The Internal Audit Department (Internal Audit) completed the FY 2025 Internal Quality
Assessment for the period of July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025.

Recommendation

Receive and file.


Strategic Commitment


This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Modernizing Business Practices: We will improve our operational efficiency through
      transparency, objective metrics, and streamlined governance, reducing over-reliance on
      subsidy while bringing our system into a state of good repair and investing in the
      development of our employees. The annual quality assurance and improvement program
      will help Internal Audit identify areas of improvement to ensure compliance with the
      auditing professional standards.


Background

Internal Audit is required to follow two sets of professional standards: the Government
Accountability Office’s (GAO) Generally Accepted Government Auditing Standards (GAGAS)
and the Institute of Internal Auditors' (IIA) Global Internal Audit Standards (Standards).


                                                                                                   114

These standards serve as the fundamental framework for all the department’s operations and
audit activities, ensuring professionalism, independence, and the highest quality of work.

To maintain this quality, the auditing standards—specifically GAGAS, Chapter 5: Quality
Control and Peer Review, and the Global Internal Audit Standards, Principle 12: Enhance
Quality—require Internal Audit to develop and maintain a Quality Assurance and Improvement
Program (QAIP). This program is comprised of both internal and external quality assessments.
The internal assessments include continuous monitoring and periodic self-assessments to
ensure the function's conformance with the professional standards. External assessments
provide an independent review to ensure the department is meeting the professional
standards.

Internal Audit conducts an annual internal quality assessment and presents the results to the
Board of Directors.


Discussion

For Fiscal Year (FY) 2025, the Internal Audit department completed its internal quality
assessment, evaluating all work performed during the fiscal year that ended on June 30, 2025.

The department’s last external independent peer review was conducted in March 2023 by the
Association of Local Government Auditors (ALGA). This review covered the period from
January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2022, and was reported to the Board in April 2023 with no
findings.

A new external peer review is scheduled for February 2026, covering the period from January
1, 2023, to December 31, 2025.

Objectives
The primary objective of our internal quality assessment was to confirm that Internal Audit's
quality control system is working effectively. This provides reasonable assurance that we
consistently follow our established policies, procedures, and relevant professional standards.

Specifically, the assessment aimed to determine if:
     Our internal policies and procedures for quality control are well-designed and followed in
     practice.
     Our auditors adhere to professional standards.

Our review included an evaluation of four audit engagements. The FY 2025 assessment
focused on engagement reports issued between July 1, 2024, and June 30, 2025. We also
examined our continuing education requirements, the Internal Audit Charter, our Internal Audit
Policy, and the Audit Procedures Handbook. The review was conducted independently by
members of the Internal Audit team.

Conclusion
Based on our completed internal quality assessment, we found no significant findings or
deficiencies. This outcome provides reasonable assurance that the department's system of
quality control is suitably designed and operating effectively in conformance with the Global


                                                                                                  115

Internal Audit Standards and Government Auditing Standards (GAGAS).


Next Steps

The results of the FY 2026 internal assessment will be reported to the Board upon its
completion.

Additionally, the next external independent peer review is tentatively scheduled for February
2026. This review will cover the period from January 1, 2023, to December 31, 2025. The
result will be reported to the Board upon completion.

Approved by:              Elisabeth Lazuardi, Director, Audit

External Quality Control Review (Peer Review): Internal Audit is required to undergo an external
quality control review (peer review) every three years to comply with the auditing standards
(Generally Accepted Government Auditing Standards (GAGAS) 3 and the 2024 Global Internal Audit
Standards). 4 There is no cost to the Authority for the peer review due to the reciprocal arrangement
that Internal Audit has with the peer review organization called the “Association of Local
Government Auditors” (ALGA).

The next Peer Review of SCRRA’s Internal Audit Department will occur during FY2026. Internal Audit
allocated hours in FY 2026 for the required peer review.

Internal Audit Administration: Refers to the range of administrative activities carried out within
the internal audit function. These activities encompass a variety of tasks, including, but not limited
to:

    •   Staff Meetings: Regular audit team meetings are held to discuss ongoing audits, share
        insights, and plan future audit activities. The Director, Audit, also attends periodic executive
        meetings and has regular one-on-one meetings with executive members, the Board chair,
        and the Audit & Finance Committee Chair & Vice Chair.
    •   Board Reporting: Preparing and presenting audit activities to the Audit & Finance Committee
        and Board of Directors.
    •   Budget Development, On-Call Audit Services contract management, and Monitoring: The
        creation of the department’s annual budget and the ongoing tracking of actual expenses
        against the budget, along with the ongoing audit bench contract management.
    •   Training: Continuous professional development activities to enhance the skills and
        knowledge of the audit team.
    •   Ethics Hotline Administration: Overseeing the agency's ethics hotline with the assistance of
        General Counsel. Internal Audit policy IA-1.2 governs the Ethics Hotline.

3
 Generally Accepted Government Auditing Standards (GAGAS), also known as the "Yellow Book," are the standards
developed by the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) for conducting government audits.

4

SUBJECT:                  Amendment to FY2025-26 Operating Budget to Carry Forward
                          Funding Amounts Remaining on the San Clemente Landslide
                          Stabilization Projects at June 30, 2025


Issue

Continuing activities at the four San Clemente slide locations, Cyprus Shores, Casa
Romantica, Mariposa and Coastal Stabilization Areas 1, 2 & 4 re quire the remainder of funds
approved for each project in prior year budgets to be carried forward to the FY26 Budget.

Recommendation

Audit and Finance Committee recommended (3-0) the Board approve the Amendment to the
FY2025-26 Budget to carry forward the funding for continuing expenses of the San Clemente
Projects at Cyprus Shores (Mile Post (MP) 206.8), Casa Romantica (MP 204.6), and Mariposa
(MP 204.2), and Coastal Stabilization Areas 1, 2 & 4.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Safety is Foundational: We will stay on the leading edge by deploying new
      technologies and processes to enhance the safety and security of our riders, our fellow
      employees, and the communities we serve. Immediate response to slide incidents in San
      Clemente were emblematic of our ongoing commitment to safety.




                                                                                                   65

Background

San Clemente #1 (Cyprus Shores)
An active landslide was identified on September 11, 2021, at Mile Post (MP) 206.8 in the City
of San Clemente. On October 22, 2021, the Board adopted an Amendment to the FY22
Budget to add $5.0M for emergency work. In FY23, $4.5M was added in an additional
Amendment bringing the total budgeted amount to $9.5M.

San Clemente #2 (Casa Romantica)
On June 23, 2023, the Board authorized emergency work in response to a landslide to protect
the track at MP 204.6 in San Clemente and approved an Amendment of $6.0M to cover the
emergency work.

San Clemente #3 (Mariposa)
On February 23, 2024, the Board adopted an Amendment to the FY24 Budget to add $9.2M to
the FY24 Budget to provide funds for emergency work at MP 204.2 in San Clemente. Orange
County Transportation Authority has requested $300K to be reserved for their expenses.

Coastal Stabilization - Areas 1, 2, 4
On April 25, 2025, the Board adopted an Amendment to the FY25 Budget to add $10.0M to
the FY25 Budget to provide funds for emergency work for Coastal Stabilization in Areas 1, 2,
4. Orange County Transportation Authority has requested $1,746,000 to be reserved for their
expenses.

Although the immediate problems are believed to be under control and service in all areas has
resumed, additional funds are needed to continue to monitor the tracks for movement and
complete various aspects of the projects. All funds will be provided by Orange County
Transportation Authority and the State of California.


Discussion

The amounts by which the FY26 Budget would be amended are as follows:
     San Clemente #1 (Cyprus Shores MP 206.8) Project #205305: $1,462,702
     San Clemente #2 (Casa Romantica MP 204.6) Project #205306: $2,829,628
     San Clemente #3 (Mariposa MP 204.2) Project #205307: $3,577,160
     Coastal Stabilization - Areas 1, 2, 4 Project #205308: $3,184,000

     San Clemente #1 (Cyprus Shores)
     Approval of this amendment will carryforward "San Clemente #1" in FY26 below the
     operating line by $1,462,702.
     San Clemente #2 (Casa Romantica)
     Approval of the amendment will carryforward "San Clemente #2" in FY26 below the
     operating line by $2,829,628.
     San Clemente #3 (Mariposa)
     Approval of the amendment will carryforward "San Clemente #3" in FY26 below the
     operating line by $3,577,160.

ITEM ID:                   2025-265-0

TO:                        Board of Directors

FROM:                      Justin Fornelli, Chief, Program Delivery


SUBJECT:                   Cooperative     Agreement      between    Orange     County
                           Transportation Authority, the City of San Clemente and the
                           Authority for the Pedestrian Audible Warning System (PAWS)
                           Rehabilitation


Issue

Approval is required to execute the Cooperative Agreement between the Orange County
Transportation Authority, City of San Clemente and the Authority for the Pedestrian Audible
Warning System (PAWS) Rehabilitation.

Recommendation

Contracts, Operations, Maintenance, and Safety Committee recommended (4-0) that the
Board authorize the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and execute the Cooperative
Agreement between the Orange County Transportation Authority (OCTA), City of San
Clemente and the Authority that will provide $1,818,000 of OCTA funding for Authority support
services to the Pedestrian Audible Warning System (PAWS) Rehabilitation.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Safety is Foundational: We will stay on the leading edge by deploying new
      technologies and processes to enhance the safety and security of our riders, our fellow
      employees, and the communities we serve. The Authority’s support to the rehabilitation
      of the PAWS system will ensure that all work will be undertaken in compliance with
      Authority safety practices, standards and criteria to maintain safe and reliable operation
      of the railroad.



                                                                                                      103

Background

In 2016, the Authority and the City entered into a Construction and Maintenance Agreement
(C&M) to install a Pedestrian Audible Warning System (PAWS) at seven (7) pedestrian
crossings along the San Clemente Beach Trail, including Dije, El Portal, Corto, T-Street, Lost
Winds, and Calafia, and at the highway-rail at-grade crossing at the San Clemente Pier,
between MP 203.9 and MP 206.0 on the Orange Subdivision. Since installation, the City has
been responsible for the operation, maintenance, and repair of the PAWS and all associated
costs, including reimbursing the Authority for any signal-related work on PAWS components
housed within the Authority’s signal system or that require interfacing with the Authority’s rail
operations.

The existing PAWS control equipment has become technologically obsolete, making spare
parts difficult or impossible to obtain, and thereby compromising the system’s reliability and
maintenance viability. The City now intends to upgrade and replace only the necessary control
equipment at each PAWS pedestrian crossing while preserving its functional components,
namely, the existing bollards, speaker systems, equipment enclosures, and flashing red “X”
signals, with OCTA funding 88 percent (88%) and the City 12 percent (12%) of the
rehabilitation costs. The City is undertaking the design for the rehabilitation scope, with OCTA
and the City requesting that the Authority undertake the construction, testing and
commissioning for the rehabilitation through the Authority’s On-Call Communication and Signal
Systems Installation Services Contract, to provide the fastest and most efficient
implementation of the scope and ensure continued reliability of the warning system.


Discussion

The Cooperative Agreement between OCTA, the City of San Clemente and the Authority
addresses the roles and responsibilities of all parties through implementation of the
rehabilitation and provides $1,818,000 of OCTA funding for Authority support services to
include Project Management, procurement, installation, testing and integration of the upgraded
PAWS control equipment, site oversight and provision of Railroad Operational Protection
throughout the rehabilitation period. Upon Agreement execution, OCTA shall deposit $900,000
with the Authority, with the remaining balance being deposited thirty (30) days prior to
construction commencement. Authority support to the project is essential to ensure that all
work will be undertaken in compliance with Authority safety practices, standards and criteria to
maintain safe and reliable operation of the safety systems, railroad and passenger services
through the location.

Rehabilitation of the PAWS system is expected to commence upon execution of the
Agreement and be completed by the end of 2025, with the Authority then continuing to operate
and maintain the signal system and the City operating and maintaining the PAWS system.

OCTA’s Transit Committee recommended execution of the Cooperative Agreement at their
July 10, 2025 Committee Meeting, with the Agreement being presented for approval to
OCTA's July 14, 2025 Board Meeting.




                                                                                                    104

Budget Impact

There is no budgetary impact as a result of this report since this is a Third Party funded
Agreement. Cash flow impact will be mitigated by an advance deposit as described in the
discussion section.


Next Steps

Upon Board Authorization, the Cooperative Agreement for the Pedestrian Audible Warning
System (PAWS) Rehabilitation. will be executed by all parties.

FROM:                      Justin Fornelli, Chief, Program Delivery


SUBJECT:                   Amendment No. 1 to Cooperative Agreement No. 23-33-021
                           with the Riverside County Transportation Commission for
                           SCRRA Design Oversight of the Perris Valley Line Double
                           Track Project


Issue

Additional RCTC-provided funding is needed to allow the Authority to support RCTC efforts to
complete the design of the Perris Valley Line Doule Track Project.

Recommendation

Contracts, Operations, Maintenance, and Safety Committee recommended (4-0) that the
Board authorize the Chief Executive Officer to negotiate and execute Amendment No. 1 to
Cooperative Agreement No. 23-33-021 between the Riverside County Transportation
Commission (RCTC) and the Authority to increase RCTC-provided funding in the amount of
$574,320, from an amount of $488,400, for a new not-to-exceed total of $1,062,720 for
Authority support on the project.


Strategic Commitment

This report aligns with the Strategic Business Plan commitment of:

      Modernizing Business Practices: We will improve our operational efficiency, through
      transparency, objective metrics and streamlined governance, reducing reliance on
      subsidy while bringing our system into a state of good repair and investing in the
      development of our employees. Completion of the Perris Valley Line Double Track
      Project will upgrade the existing freight track that is in poor condition and cannot run
      Metrolink service, and replace existing turnouts, install new signal systems and integrate



                                                                                                      106

     into the PTC network.


Background

The Perris Valley Line Double Track Project is an RCTC-led project to upgrade the existing,
non-functional second track and replace existing turnouts, install new signal systems and
integrate into the PTC network. The track segment extends the recent upgraded track through
Moreno Valley/March Field station. As RCTC advances the project, the Authority's continued
support is needed. At RCTC's Board of Directors meeting in October 2022, and subsequently
at the Authority's Board of Directors meeting on March 29, 2024, Cooperative Agreement No.
23-33-021 was approved by both parties. The Agreement defined the roles and responsibilities
of each party and provided initial funding for Authority support on the project.


Discussion

As the project has progressed, several factors were identified that expanded the project's
scope, cost, and schedule. Increased oversight by the Authority is required to assess
condition of the existing track, review existing turnouts, install new signals at each turnout,
complete environmental studies to meet federal environmental requirements, and support the
design. Additional RCTC-provided funding is needed to allow the Authority to complete these
efforts.

This Amendment to Agreement No. 23-33-021 was approved by the RCTC Board of Directors
on June 11, 2025.


Budget Impact

There is no budget impact as this is a Third Party funded Agreement. To address Authority
cash flow constraints, RCTC staff have agreed to provide a deposit of 50% of the Amendment
#1 amount once the agreement is executed.


Next Steps

Upon Board authorization, Amendment No. 1 to Cooperative Agreement No. 23-33-021-01 will
be executed by both parties.
